    `RTCPeerConnection::set_multicast_dns_destination_reported`, `Agent::...`, `Mdns::
    set_destination_reported`), a group address in `local_addr` is an arrival at the group.
    Before, only `Mdns::handle_datagram` applied it, so through a peer connection a LAN of
    public addresses resolved no `.local` name. `PeerDriver` declares it and reports each mDNS
    datagram's destination where it knows it (Linux IPv4, bound to the group; a runtime that
    fills `RecvMeta::dst_ip`); unknown elsewhere (tokio, smol: no `IP_PKTINFO` read), where the
    scope of the source still decides.
  - Under `QueryAndGather` a local peer-reflexive candidate (RFC 8445 7.2.5.3.1) no longer shows
    its base in the related address, and one whose mapped address is a hidden host address
    shows the host's name (draft-ietf-mmusic-mdns-ice-candidates 3.3.1, first MUST).
  - `RTCIceCandidate`'s string form ran the related address into the port
    (`udp prflx 10.1.0.135:55410172.17.0.1`); it now reads `... related 172.17.0.1:40000`.
  - The process's mDNS budget can be set once before first use
    (`peer::set_process_mdns_rate_limit`); a driver on a runtime with a virtual clock
    (`Runtime::virtual_clock`, new, `true` for `MockRuntime`) takes from a budget of its own
    instead of the process's wall-clock one, so a mock clock can neither empty it for real
    drivers nor wait on it.
  - F9 decided: QU stays off with the driver (its IPv4 socket on Linux is bound to the group
    and receives no unicast; RFC 6762 section 15.1).
  Tests: `mdns_answer_trust_test.rs::test_a_reported_multicast_destination_in_local_addr_makes_a_public_source_on_link`,
  `mdns_virtual_time.rs::drivers_on_a_lan_of_public_addresses_resolve_each_other`,
  `agent_checklist_test.rs::test_a_local_peer_reflexive_candidate_does_not_show_a_hidden_host_address`,
  `candidate.rs::the_string_form_separates_the_related_address_from_the_port`,
  `tests/mdns_budget.rs`. Engine behaviour change (rtci-mdns trust with a reported
  destination; rtci-ice local peer-reflexive candidates; the candidate string form).

### Changed

- SRTP re-keying (RFC 5764 section 4.4) starts at a margin measured in time as well as in
  packets: the larger of a sixteenth of the key's lifetime and the packets the key protects,
  at the rate it has been used since its first packet, in the time a re-keying needs as
  measured on the handshake that gave it (twice the handshake's duration, for the handshake
  and the ICE checks of the restart, plus one DTLS retransmission timer). On a slow path with
  a short lifetime the re-keying starts earlier instead of the key running out and the
  transport failing (0.1.0's known limit); with the default lifetimes, and wherever the
  sixteenth is the larger, nothing moves. `OnSrtpKeyLifetimeExpiring` still comes at the
  sixteenth; the DTLS client still asks first (`with_srtp_rekeying_dtls_client_first`: the
  client measures its handshake from its first flight, the server from the first datagram it
  reads). Engine behaviour change.

- **conformance** (sctp-20): nine RFC 9260 rows the code had already caught up with are closed
  with their tests, each checked by mutation: the ABORT with Unresolvable Address (3.3.2), the
  negotiated stream count (5.1.1), the stale cookie of a restart or collision (5.2.4, SHOULD),
  route changes (7.2.5.2), the protocol parameters and failure threshold as settings (11.1),
  and the COOKIE ACK bundled with the SACK for the DATA that came with the cookie (3.3.12,
  5.1, 5.1.5; the test now checks the one packet). Supported Address Types in INIT (5.1.2) is
  `n/a`: RFC 8261 6.1 forbids it over DTLS. Engine behaviour change: no.

- **A video RED format is not negotiated without ULPFEC (RFC 5109 section 14.3).** "In
  cases in which the redundancy payload format is used with FEC as the only secondary codec,
  when the FEC stream is rejected the redundant encoding payload type SHOULD also be
  removed": a `video/red` format without an fmtp line (it names no encodings, so ULPFEC is
  the only thing it can carry) is left out of the negotiated formats when no `ulpfec` format
  of its rate is negotiated, and the RTX format that names it goes too. This changes the
  answer of an application that registered `video/red` and not `ulpfec`; the default codecs
  register neither, and audio RED is untouched.
- A new m= section that an offer keeps outside every BUNDLE group although the offer has
  groups (`RTCRtpTransceiver::set_bundle_request(Some(false))` on a transceiver the last
  answer did not have) gets a transport of its own, as the method's documentation says; it
  was put on the BUNDLE transport. A section a description leaves outside every group is
  never written `a=bundle-only`.

- **sctp** (sctp-18): `AssociationStats` counts DATA chunks sent again
  (`get_num_retransmissions`), messages abandoned (`get_num_abandoned_messages`), losses Fast
  Retransmit found in messages whose retransmission budget was spent and abandoned instead
  (`get_num_fast_retrans_abandoned`), FORWARD TSN chunks sent (`get_num_forward_tsns`) and the
  time T3-rtx expiries waited (`get_t3_wait`, the RTO at each expiry); `RTCSctpTransport::
  association_stats` gives them for the live association (a diagnostic, not a W3C member). The
  documentation of `get_num_datas` said "sent"; it counts DATA chunks received.
- **tests** (sctp-18): the test environment's 1000-message unreliable channel at 10 % loss
  (`testenv_impairment::unreliable_channel_loses_without_retransmitting`) asserts on counted
  protocol events: no DATA of the channel sent twice, every lost message abandoned and
  skipped with FORWARD TSN, at least 45 % of the losses found by Fast Retransmit, T3-rtx
  expiries at most 3/4 of the losses and their mean wait at most 3 s, and the time not spent
  waiting for T3-rtx under 40 s; the wall time is a 120 s ceiling only (was the assertion, at
  90 s). It prints the T3-rtx expiries and their wait beside the drain figure. Engine
  behaviour change: no (counters only).

- **sctp** (sctp-24, pass2): the INIT sent after a Stale Cookie ERROR carries a Cookie
  Preservative (RFC 9260 3.3.2.1.3, 5.2.6) asking for what the cookie was late by, at least
  the round trip of the COOKIE ECHO / ERROR exchange and at most a second beyond it (the 5.2.6
  SHOULD); `AssociationStats::get_num_sack_losses` counts SACKs found lost from Duplicate TSN
  reports of timer retransmissions (6.2 MAY). RFC9260-3.3.2.1.3-1, 5.2.6-3, 6.2-25 are
  `tested`. Engine behaviour change: yes, small (a 8-byte parameter in an INIT that follows a
  stale cookie; a counter).
- **sctp** (sctp-23, pass2): an association that ends with user messages it did not deliver reports them (RFC
  9260 8.1: "report the failure to the upper layer and optionally report back all
  outstanding user data"): one `Event::SendFailure { unsent, unacknowledged }` (11.2.2)
  before `AssociationClosed`, and `Association::take_undelivered_messages()` hands back each
  message (`UndeliveredMessage`: stream, SSN, PPI, unordered, mode `Unsent` /
  `Unacknowledged`, partial flag, the bytes not acknowledged) as Receive Unsent / Receive
  Unacknowledged Message do (11.1.14, 11.1.15). A graceful shutdown leaves none.
- **sctp** (sctp-23, pass2): `Event::CommunicationError { causes }` for each ERROR chunk the peer sends (11.2.5),
  `ErrorCauseCode::value()`; `Association::request_heartbeat(now)` (11.1.10, also with
  heartbeats disabled); `Association::status()` (`AssociationStatus`, 11.1.8) and
  `peer_receive_window()`. RFC9260-8.1-5, 11.1-2, 11.1-3, 11.1-5, 11.2-2 are `tested`.
  Engine behaviour change: new events only (both `Event` variants under `#[non_exhaustive]`);
  the outbound queues of an ended association are emptied into the undelivered list.
- **sctp** (sctp-19): three optional behaviours of RFC 9260. A SHUTDOWN goes with a SACK when
  what was received has gaps, which the SHUTDOWN's Cumulative TSN Ack cannot report (3.3.8);
  the last DATA chunk sent in SHUTDOWN-PENDING carries the I bit, so the receiver acknowledges
  it without the SACK delay the SHUTDOWN waits for (3.3.1, RFC 7053); and
  `TransportConfig::with_fragmentation(false)` turns fragmentation off, refusing a message
  larger than one DATA chunk of a full-sized packet with `ErrOutboundPacketTooLarge` (6.9; on
  by default). Engine behaviour change (shutdown packets): yes. The answer to a refused INIT
  (an ABORT to its Initiate Tag, 3.3.2) was already there; its audit row is closed with its
  test.

### Features

- **SettingEngineBuilder::with_wall_clock** (`conf/jsep-75-session-version`): the wall-clock
  time paired with the instant the peer connection is built, for the values it writes on the
  wall clock itself: the `o=` session version, the receivers' source timestamps and the NTP
  times of the RTCP session it installs. With a seeded crypto provider the `o=` line is the
  same in every run under virtual time. Also `sdp::description::session::Origin::jsep`,
  `SessionDescription::new_jsep_session_description_with_origin` and
  `NTP_UNIX_EPOCH_OFFSET_SECS`.

- **SettingEngineBuilder::with_rtcp_mux_only_in_subsequent_offers** (`conf/jsep-76-spec-conflicts`):
  RFC 8858 section 4.5's form, a subsequent offer saying `a=rtcp-mux-only` again in the m=
  sections it carries over (under the `require` mux policy; in the tagged section, or in every
  bundled one with the bundle attributes repeated). Off by default and in the `Rfc` and
  `Chrome` profiles, on in `StrictRfc`: RFC 9429 section 5.2.2, which governs a JSEP endpoint,
  says "The 'a=rtcp-mux-only' line MUST NOT be added". No change to what the engine generates
  by default. RFC8858-4.5-1 is `conflict` (was `violated`), with
  `tests/jsep_rtcp_mux.rs::when_asked_a_subsequent_offer_says_rtcp_mux_only_again`; RFC8858-4.5-4
  is `n/a`.
- **jsep**: RFC9429-4.1.1-4 (ignore `max-bundle`) is `conflict` (was `violated`): the existing
  `with_max_bundle_as_must_bundle(false)` is RFC 9429's form and the default is W3C
  webrtc-pc 4.2.5's; the test is split in two, one per form
  (`tests/jsep_bundle_policy.rs::max_bundle_selects_must_bundle_by_default`,
  `max_bundle_is_ignored_when_set_to_be_ignored`).

- **rtci-sdp**: typed `Tool`, `ConferenceType`, `Orient` and `Quality` attributes with
  `SessionDescription::tool`, `conference_type` and `MediaDescription::orient`, `quality`
  (`conf/jsep-78-sdp-informational`); the SDP fuzz targets cover them. RFC8866-6.3-1, 6.8-1,
  6.9-1, 6.14-1 and 6.7-1 are `tested`, 6.4-1, 6.5-1 and 5.8-7 too (their notes were stale).

- **A connection can take an existing connection's RTCP CNAME (RFC 8834 section 4.9 MAY).**
  `RTCPeerConnectionBuilder::with_rtcp_cname(existing.rtcp_cname())`: "if explicitly
  requested at creation, an RTCPeerConnection MAY use the same CNAME as an existing
  RTCPeerConnection", so a receiver can synchronise the streams of both. Without it each
  connection generates its own (unchanged). A CNAME outside 1 to 255 octets fails `build`
  with the new `Error::ErrRtcpCnameLength`. Audit: RFC8834-4.9-5 `tested`; with new tests
  RFC8835-4.2-8 (bundling by media type), RFC8837-5-6 (AF3x for non-interactive video) and
  the stale RFC8834-8-2 (RTCP XR generation) `tested`.

- **statistics** (`conf/vp-4-engine-boundary`): `DecoderStatsUpdate` has four new public
  fields, `jitter_buffer_delay`, `jitter_buffer_target_delay`, `jitter_buffer_minimum_delay` and
  `jitter_buffer_emitted_count`: a struct literal without `..Default::default()` needs them.

- **video pipeline, phase 3: the send pipeline** (`conf/vp-7-send`, `docs/video-pipeline.md`
  6.5; built on `conf/gcc-5-app-limited`, merged in, for the pacer's pause and discards):
  - `rtci_video::send::SendPipeline`: pictures in, RTP packets out (the negotiated codec's
    payloader, timestamps from the capture time). The target (`RTCRtpSender::target_bitrates`,
    the estimate less the retransmission reserve) sets the encoder's rate, never below the
    encoder's minimum (pictures dropped in the ratio target / minimum instead); a target of 0
    (the pacer's pause) stops the encoder, and the first picture after it is coded as it
    comes (`conf/vp-9-no-keyframe-on-resume`, below);
    PLI, FIR and the pacer's discards ask for a key frame, not served within two round trips
    of the last one (RFC 5104 3.5.1; 500 ms until a round trip is known, RFC 7728 8.1);
    resolution and frame-rate steps when the target falls under what the format needs, in the
    order of the W3C `degradationPreference` (default `balanced`), with a 5 s hold before a
    step back up. `SendConfig::chrome()`: libwebrtc's choices (one request served per 300 ms,
    `maintain-framerate`).
  - `rtci_video::engine::VideoSender`: the glue to an `RTCRtpSender` (target, events, round
    trip, `update_encoder_stats` with `qualityLimitation*`).
  - `VideoEncoder::set_rates` and `min_bitrate_bps` (both with defaults), `EncoderFactory`,
    `picture::scale_into`.
  - Breaking for an exhaustive `match` (`rtci-video` is not published): `engine::Error` has a
    new variant `Encode`.
  - Measured with the VP8 backend in a two-peer call on the default interceptors (640x360,
    30 fps): open link, encoded rate within 0.1 % of the target over 10 s windows; the capacity
    test's 300 kbit/s cap on six seeds, longest freeze 1.19 to 1.71 s, 0 frames discarded by
    the pacer, 0 pictures encoded in a pause, a key frame after each, 1186 to 1385 kbit/s 20 s
    after the cap; known cost: the oldest picture shown is 10.2 to 11.7 s old after the cap
    (the pacer's backlog of the 2.5 Mbit/s before the estimate fell); 2 % loss repaired by
    NACK with no wait beyond the slowest repair. Each reaction mutation-checked.
  - Not built yet: simulcast, temporal layers and SVC, the rate allocators, the encoder bitrate
    adjuster, the zero-hertz cadence adapter.

- **video pipeline: codec safety** (`conf/vp-6-codec-safety`, `docs/video-pipeline.md` 4.7,
  4.8, 6.4):
  - Breaking: `rtci-video`'s `vp8` feature is opt-in again (default features: `engine`). The
    default build decodes no video until the application enables a codec. Supply-chain review
    of `vp8-decoder` / `vp8-encoder` 0.1.3 (publisher, contents against the tagged commit,
    `unsafe`, build-time code, licences, prior art) with a recommendation for the owner;
    `scripts/check-video-codec-pins.py` fails on any other version or checksum.
  - `codec::av1`: the 96-byte leak found by fuzzing is rav1d 1.1.0's (memorysafety/rav1d#1522:
    every `dav1d_picture_unref` and every empty `dav1d_get_picture` leaves a 48-byte `Arc`;
    about 50 to 100 bytes a frame), documented on the feature. Separately, a temporal unit's
    `Dav1dData` is now released when taking out a waiting picture fails (found by reading).
    The abort on hostile input is rav1d 1.1.0's (memorysafety/rav1d#1497, fixed on its
    main branch, unreleased), documented on the feature in plain words; reproducer in
    `rtci-video/tests/data/rav1d-abort.ivf`.
  - Feature `isolation`: `codec::isolated::IsolatedDecoder` runs any decoder in a child process
    (`serve` on the child's side); a child that aborts, crashes or hangs costs that frame.
  - `codec::vp8` catches a panic of the decoder and replaces it (`DecodeError::Corrupt`).
  - Features `libvpx` (VP8 / VP9 decode and encode), `dav1d` (AV1 decode) and `openh264`
    (H.264 decode and encode with Cisco's binary only, accepted by its published SHA-256): each
    loads its library at run time, so building them needs no system library (`cargo check
    --all-features` stays pure Rust). libvpx's decode of the VP8 fixture equals libvpx's
    reference output; libdav1d survives every single-bit flip of a key frame (19,352) and 1500
    seeded mutations that abort rav1d. The AV1 wrappers no longer refuse a key frame after an
    accepted hostile delta frame (an error met while taking out a waiting picture is the
    earlier unit's). A CI job installing the libraries is proposed, not added.
  - The root crate no longer dev-depends on `rtci-video`: the interop peer's `pipeline`
    scenario is built by the new `rtci-video-interop` package (feature `pipeline`, binary
    `interop-peer-video`, which the browser stage now starts), so workspace builds compile no
    codec.

- **video pipeline, phase 2: codecs** (`conf/vp-5-codecs`, `docs/video-pipeline.md` 4.6):
  - `rtci-video` feature `vp8` (default): VP8 decode and encode in pure Rust with
    `vp8-decoder` / `vp8-encoder` pinned to `=0.1.3`. Checked on hosted runners: the WebM
    project's 59 VP8 test vectors bit-exact, libvpx's decode of the same streams identical
    (58 of 60; the two others change resolution, which the comparison tool rescales), every
    encoded stream decoded identically by libvpx, 720p decode at 257 fps or more and encode at
    53 fps or more on one core, 15 min of libFuzzer with no finding.
  - Feature `av1` (opt-in): AV1 decode with `rav1d` and encode with `rav1e`, both without
    assembly. rav1d matches dav1d on libaom's vectors (10 of 10) and decodes 720p at about
    40 fps, but aborts the process on a hostile frame (a panic across its C API); rav1e makes
    5 to 8 pictures a second at 360p (not real time) and holds 4 pictures back.
  - `picture` (I420 view and buffer, PSNR, a synthetic source), the `encoder::VideoEncoder`
    trait, `VideoDecoder::picture`, `codec::decoder_for`.
  - Tests: PSNR at 640x360 and 600 kbit/s (VP8 39.5 dB), hostile VP8 frames (no panic), the
    libvpx fixture's MD5, the VP8 fixture and a rav1e stream through loss decoded bit-exactly,
    a two-peer call with the real VP8 codecs. `scripts/video-codec-check.sh` and
    `rtci-video/examples/codec_check.rs` reproduce the evidence.
  - interop-peer scenario `{"media":"pipeline","video":"VP8"|"AV1"}` and the browser cells
    `pipeline receive VP8` / `AV1`; the root crate dev-depends on `rtci-video` (path only).
  - `deny.toml`: libfuzzer-sys (NCSA, a permissive licence) allowed; it is a `cfg(fuzzing)`-only
    dependency of rav1e. The dev profile optimises the codec crates (their tests code video).

- **video pipeline, phase 1b: the engine boundary** (`conf/vp-4-engine-boundary`,
  `docs/video-pipeline.md` 2.6, 2.9):
  - `RTCRtpReceiver::set_nack_horizon(now, ssrc, oldest_useful)` and
    `interceptor::NackControl::Horizon`: the receiving application tells the NACK generator the
    oldest sequence number it can still use (RFC 4588 6.3: a retransmission is asked for only
    while it "would still be useful"); the generator asks for no older missing packet and
    forgets its requests for them (wrap-aware; `None` removes the horizon)
    (`packets_older_than_the_horizon_are_not_asked_for`,
    `a_receiver_stops_asking_for_packets_behind_its_nack_horizon`). The RTCP session drops
    them from a NACK it still holds for its next packet as well (RFC 4585 3.5.2, step 4a:
    stored feedback is sent only if it is still useful), and sends no NACK that is left
    asking for nothing: before, a request made just ahead of the horizon left with the next
    regular RTCP packet, up to about two seconds after the application had given the packet
    up (`conf/vp-9r2-vp8-partitions`;
    `a_nack_held_for_the_regular_packet_drops_what_the_nack_horizon_passed`). `rtci_video::engine::
    VideoReceiver::poll` moves it on after every released picture (`ReceiveConfig::
    nack_horizon`, on by default, as libwebrtc's `NackRequester::ClearUpTo`).
  - The jitter buffer members (`jitterBufferDelay`, `jitterBufferTargetDelay`,
    `jitterBufferMinimumDelay`, `jitterBufferEmittedCount`) in `DecoderStatsUpdate`, winning over
    the audio update's (`the_decoder_update_carries_the_jitter_buffer_members_of_a_video_stream`);
    `rtci-video` no longer goes through `update_audio_receiver_stats`.
  - `rtci-video`'s two-peer tests trace every lost packet (gap seen, first NACK, RTX sent and
    arrived) and count NACKs for packets behind the horizon (none, asserted in the capacity
    scenario); `docs/video-repair-latency.md` holds the trace.

- **video pipeline, phase one: the receive side** (`conf/vp-2-receive`, design on
  `conf/vp-1-design`, `docs/video-pipeline.md`; on master by `conf/vp-3-on-master`). A new
  crate, `rtci-video`, sans-I/O, pure Rust, no codec dependency, not published with 0.1.0
  (`publish = false`):
  - `assembly::PacketBuffer`: frames from RTP packets per payload format (VP8 S / PID, VP9
    B / E, AV1 and the Dependency Descriptor's start / end of frame, H.264 / H.265 by RTP
    timestamp and marker), key frames and key-frame sizes, duplicates, late packets, overflow
    and backward jumps as libwebrtc's `packet_buffer.cc`.
  - `reference::ReferenceFinder`: frame ids and references with libwebrtc's dispatch: VP8
    temporal layers (TL0PICIDX, TID, Y), picture-id-only and sequence-number-only streams
    (padding closes gaps), VP9 flexible mode with inter-layer dependency and non-flexible
    picture groups, the Dependency Descriptor's fdiffs.
  - `buffer::FrameBuffer`: decodable temporal units, dropping of frames passed over
    (`framesDropped`, `packetsDiscarded`), libwebrtc's limits (800 frames, 8192 decoded ids).
  - `timing`: ports of libwebrtc's jitter estimator (Kalman filter on frame delay variation
    and size, noise threshold, retransmission term, frame-rate scaling), timestamp
    extrapolator, decode-time percentile and render-time model, the playout-delay extension,
    `jitterBufferTarget` and an A/V sync delay input; release at render time minus decode and
    render time, late pictures skipped (`kMaxAllowedFrameDelay`), the low-latency path.
  - `keyframe::KeyFramePolicy`: PLI on a first frame that is not a key frame, packet buffer
    overflow, a missing Dependency Descriptor structure, the decode timeouts (200 ms / 3 s, or
    from `rtx-time`), decoder errors, repeated every 200 ms until a key frame decodes, and a
    repair window (5 RTT, at least 1 s) after which pictures stuck behind a gap ask for a key
    frame (`ReceiveConfig::chrome()` keeps libwebrtc's decode timeout only).
  - `render::RenderStats`: W3C `freezeCount`, `totalFreezesDuration`, `pauseCount`,
    `totalPausesDuration`, `totalInterFrameDelay`, `totalSquaredInterFrameDelay`,
    `framesRendered` (W3C definition; libwebrtc's 5-interval warm-up in `chrome()`).
  - `decoder::VideoDecoder` trait and `ReferenceCheckingDecoder`; `engine::VideoReceiver`
    (feature `engine`): one pipeline per SSRC of an `RTCRtpReceiver`, PLI through
    `write_rtcp` when `nack pli` was negotiated, `report_received_frame`, the statistics
    through `update_decoder_stats` (the jitter buffer members through
    `update_audio_receiver_stats` for now).
  - Tests: libvpx VP8 / VP9 IVF and H.264 / H.265 Annex B fixtures through 5 % loss with
    0..40 ms reordering and retransmission (every picture byte-identical, in an order the
    stream allows, no freeze); calls between two peer connections at 2 % and 10 % loss and a
    300 kbit/s capacity drop (no wait beyond the slowest repair, no corrupt picture, no
    decode out of order).

### Added

- **interceptor / bandwidth probing: recovery probing, an opt-in** (off by default and in
  every behaviour profile; ungoverned: it is tuning, no specification asks for it and Chrome
  does not do it): `ProbeController::with_recovery_probing`,
  `CongestionControlBuilder::with_recovery_probing`,
  `DefaultInterceptorOptions::recovery_probing`. A sender that keeps up with its target is
  asked nothing once the probes after a drop have ended (five seconds after it), so when a
  capacity that fell comes back, the climb is the delay-based controller's 8% a second. With
  the setting the highest rate before a large drop is remembered for a minute
  (`PROBE_DROP_MEMORY`); while the target is below 85% of it and the estimator does not read
  over-use (`BandwidthEstimator::usage`), a cluster at twice the target is asked for every
  five seconds (`PROBE_RECOVERY_INTERVAL`), with follow-ons at twice the result while the
  path carries what is asked. Paced chains only: clusters that leave as bursts are not sent
  for it, and a path change forgets the remembered rate. WHAT A CALL GAINS AND PAYS, measured
  on the capacity instrument (default chain, a 2.5 Mbit/s path that drops to 300 kbit/s for
  20 s, 200 calls a cell, hosted runs 45607015088 without and 45607025736 with the setting,
  on master f9242b4d with the two probing branches before this one): the target is back at
  1 Mbit/s 4.9 s after the limit went (5.4 s at most) instead of 17.3 s, and at the
  2.5 Mbit/s maximum 15 to 25 s after it instead of 1283 kbit/s on average; the same behind
  a 100 ms queue (17.6 -> 5.0 s) and with both directions limited (16.2 -> 4.8 s); behind a
  1000 ms queue in nine calls of ten (median 17.6 -> 5.0 s, the slowest tenth 17.5 s). It
  costs 3% of the target under the limit (238 against 246 kbit/s), and behind a 100 ms queue
  11 more audio packets lost a call (52 against 41) and a quarter more packets dropped at
  the queue (201 against 159; with the pacer's backlog kept, `PacerBacklog::Keep`, behind the
  300 ms queue 149 against 121 in the two-peer test's call); the counts of calls with an old
  picture, a freeze or an audio gap do not move in any cell. After a limit that outlasts the minute (held 60 s) it gains
  nothing: 17.6 s against 16.9 s, the rate not back within 20 s in 33 of 200 calls against
  14. Sent as bursts in a chain without a pacer the gain was the same and the calls with an
  old picture rose in every cell that had any (both directions limited: 25 -> 31 of 200), so
  the setting does not act there. The default's figures do not move. Tests: seven in
  `cc::probe::tests` (`recovery_probing_…`, `a_recovery_cluster_the_path_carries_is_followed_up`,
  `without_recovery_probing_a_sender_at_its_target_is_not_probed_after_the_drop`),
  `rtci-interceptor/tests/recovery_probing.rs`, `tests/recovery_probe_requests.rs`,
  `tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs::with_recovery_probing_a_call_is_back_at_full_rate_when_the_capacity_returns`.
- **interceptor / bandwidth probing: the probe after a large drop has three forms**
  (`AfterDropProbe`: `Repeated`, `Libwebrtc`, `Off`), set with
  `ProbeController::with_after_drop_probe`, `CongestionControlBuilder::with_after_drop_probe`
  and `DefaultInterceptorOptions::probe_after_drop`; the behaviour row `cc.probe-after-drop`
  governs it (`Rfc` and `StrictRfc`: `Repeated`; `Chrome`: `Libwebrtc`).
  `with_probe_after_drop(bool)` stays (`true` is `Repeated`, `false` is `Off`). THE DEFAULT
  DOES NOT CHANGE: `Repeated` is what the engine did (from a second after the target fell
  below two thirds of its 2 s high, once a second for five seconds, a cluster at 85% of that
  high); on the capacity instrument 1400 calls in seven cells of the default chain are
  identical to the tree before, figure for figure (hosted run 45607015088 against
  45582695439). `Libwebrtc` is libwebrtc's `ProbeController::RequestProbe`: a drop is one
  update of the estimate below 0.66 of the one before it, and one cluster at 0.85 of the
  estimate before it is asked when the delay detector has returned from under-use to normal,
  only for a sender that is application limited or was within 3 s, within 5 s of the drop, at
  most once in 5 s, and only when 95% of it is above the estimate. For it the estimator
  says how it reads the path: `BandwidthEstimator::usage() -> Usage` (new, default
  `Usage::Normal`; `Gcc`: the reading of the last feedback), passed on with
  `ProbeController::set_usage`. No specification says how to probe after a drop (RFC 8836
  section 2, 1f, asks that a flow regain its share quickly), so the default is the form that
  measured best. Four forms, the default chain, a 2.5 Mbit/s path that drops to 300 kbit/s
  for 20 s, 1000 calls in each of the two reference cells and 200 in six others, each form
  against the default by the merge-point rule of `docs/capacity-instrument.md`: without a
  probe and with libwebrtc's (which never fires for a sender that keeps up with its target:
  the two measure alike) seven figures are worse (both directions limited: oldest picture
  3.07 s against 2.64 s; 5% of the feedback lost: the rate not back within 20 s in 30 and 24
  of 200 calls against 2; target 15 to 25 s after the limit 1205 against 1278 kbit/s); the
  repeated probe aimed at the highest rate of the last minute instead of the last drop's own
  high makes fifteen worse (audio packets lost 27 -> 35 a call; behind a 1000 ms queue over
  2 s without a new picture in 33 of 200 calls against 6) and was not taken. What the default
  costs against no probe: behind a 1000 ms queue 96 audio packets lost a call against 66,
  under a limit that lasts a minute 74 against 45. Tests:
  `cc::probe::tests::libwebrtcs_probe_after_a_drop_is_one_cluster_once_overuse_has_ended`,
  `libwebrtcs_probe_after_a_drop_has_its_conditions`,
  `gcc::estimator::tests::usage_follows_the_last_feedback`,
  `rtci-interceptor/tests/after_drop_probe_requests.rs`, `tests/default_probe_after_drop.rs`.
- **congestion control feedback cadence as a setting** (rtcpbudget-2):
  `CongestionFeedbackCadence` (`ReceivedMedia`, `PerFrame`, `SendEstimate`),
  `TwccReceiverBuilder::with_cadence`, `Rfc8888Builder::with_cadence`,
  `DefaultInterceptorOptions::congestion_feedback_cadence` and the governed behaviour
  `cc.feedback-cadence`. **The default does not change**: feedback every 50 to 250 ms, sized
  to 5% of the media received (`ReceivedMedia`), which is the engine's own choice and no
  specification's. `PerFrame` is the drafts' cadence (draft-ietf-rmcat-gcc-02 section 3,
  draft-holmer-rmcat-transport-wide-cc-extensions-01 section 3: a lone video stream is
  reported when each frame ends, anything else every 30 ms, up to 100 ms where this
  endpoint's share of the RTCP bandwidth does not hold that), on in the `StrictRfc` profile;
  as the default it measured worse in the capacity instrument (send target under a 300
  kbit/s cap 210 -> 186 kbit/s, the picture requirement of the pacer-less chain missed in
  36 instead of 4 of 200 calls, RTCP 122 -> 135 kbit/s on an open call), and so did 100 ms
  always and two forms between (audit rows TWCC-3-4 and GCC-3-2: `setting`, measured).
  `SendEstimate` is libwebrtc's cadence (50 to 250 ms from 5% of the endpoint's own send
  estimate, 100 ms before one is known), **now the `Chrome` profile's** (a behaviour change
  for that profile only: its feedback was sized to the media received). New attributes on
  what the chain hands application-ward: `RtcpBandwidthShare` (this endpoint's share of the
  RTCP bandwidth, from the RTCP session) and `SendEstimate` (the congestion controller's
  estimate beside `TargetBitrateChanged`). The capacity instrument's chain token `perframe`
  runs the drafts' form.

- **interceptors** (rtcpbudget-5): an option, off by default and in every behaviour profile,
  for an endpoint's own share of the RTCP bandwidth to follow the rate its congestion
  controller allows it to send at: `RtcpSessionBuilder::with_share_following_send_rate`,
  `DefaultInterceptorOptions::rtcp_share_follows_send_rate`,
  `RtcpSessionControl::SendRate` and `CongestionControlBuilder::with_send_rate_told_to_rtcp`
  (the congestion controller tells the RTCP session of its chain the estimate whenever it has
  moved by a twentieth). **It is tuning with no specification behind it**: RFC 3550 section
  6.2 sizes the RTCP bandwidth from the session bandwidth (here the media measured both
  ways) and section 6.3.1 shares it equally among the members whatever each direction
  carries, so an endpoint whose uplink has collapsed to 300 kbit/s while the other direction
  still carries 2.5 Mbit/s keeps sending about 80 kbit/s of RTCP on it. With the option the
  endpoint's own SSRCs schedule their regular reports with at most 5% of a session in which
  every endpoint sends at this endpoint's rate (5% x send rate x members / local SSRCs, no
  less than 5% of the minimum session bandwidth); the intervals calculated for the other
  members (`RtcpReportingInterval`, what the circuit breaker takes for the peer's reporting
  interval), member timeouts, BYE and sender status keep RFC 3550's value, and congestion
  control feedback is not slowed. Measured in the capacity instrument (default chain, one
  direction capped at 300 kbit/s): RTCP on the capped link 80 -> 34 kbit/s, the open call
  unchanged (122 kbit/s); figures for the picture and the recovery are in
  `docs/capacity-instrument.md`. The `Performance` profile does not take it: its
  `T_rr_interval` of one second already brings that RTCP to 22 kbit/s, and beside it the
  option changed nothing that was measured. Tests
  `the_rtcp_share_follows_the_send_rate_the_session_is_told`,
  `the_interval_calculated_for_the_peer_does_not_follow_the_send_rate`.

- **interceptor** (collapse-2): `ProbeFill`, an attribute the pacer adds to a `ProbeRequest`'s
  carrier on its way application-ward: the padding the cluster needs beyond the media and
  retransmissions waiting in the pacer's queue. The NACK responder fills the cluster with
  that much; a chain without a pacer has no such attribute and the whole cluster is padding,
  as before.
- **interceptor** (`conf/flush-1r-backlog-flush-at-collapse`): `PacerBacklog` (`Flush`, the
  default, and `Keep`), `PacerBuilder::with_backlog`, `DefaultInterceptorOptions::pacer_backlog`,
  the notice `PacerFlush { ssrcs }` the pacer sends application-ward at a flush (the NACK
  responder forgets those streams), and `PacerInterceptor::flushes()`.
- **rtp, media** (`conf/flush-2-receiver-gap-bound`): `Depacketizer::has_key_frames()` and
  `Depacketizer::is_key_frame_start(payload)` (both with a default of `false`, so an
  implementation outside the workspace compiles unchanged): the first packet of a key frame by
  the payload format's own rule, for VP8 (P=0 in the payload header, RFC 7741 section 4.3),
  VP9 (P=0 at the start of a base-layer frame, RFC 9628 section 4.2), AV1 (the aggregation
  header's N bit), H.264 (the first slice of an IDR picture, alone, in an FU-A / FU-B or an
  STAP-A / STAP-B; `IDR_NALU_TYPE`, `SEI_NALU_TYPE`) and H.265 (the first slice segment of an
  IRAP picture, alone, in a fragmentation unit or an aggregation packet, with or without
  DONL). `SampleBuilder`: `DEFAULT_MAX_GAP_WAIT`, `with_key_frame_release(bool)`,
  `key_frame_releases() -> u64`, and `nack_horizon() -> Option<u16>` (the oldest sequence
  number still of use, for `RTCRtpReceiver::set_nack_horizon`). Tests:
  `rtci-rtp/src/codec/key_frame_start_test.rs`,
  `rtci-media/src/io/sample_builder/sample_builder_key_frame_test.rs`,
  `sample_builder_gap_wait_test.rs`.

- **interceptors** (breaker-1): `CircuitBreakerBuilder::with_automatic_restart` and
  `DefaultInterceptorOptions::circuit_breaker_automatic_restart` (on by default: RFC 8083
  section 4.5's restart on information that the congestion has dissipated; off leaves every
  restart to the application); `DefaultInterceptorOptions::circuit_breaker` and the governed
  behaviour `cb.enabled` (`Rfc` and `StrictRfc` on: RFC 8834 section 7.1; `Chrome` off:
  libwebrtc has no RTP circuit breaker); `RtcpReportingInterval`, the deterministic
  reporting interval the RTCP session calculates, attached to the RTCP it hands
  application-ward.

- **rtci, interceptor** (collapse-3): `RTCPeerConnectionEvent::OnCircuitBreaker` and
  `CircuitBreakerNotice` (see "Fixed"). An application that sends media should handle the
  event: a flow the circuit breaker ceased stays silent until the application restarts it
  (`DefaultInterceptorHandles::circuit_breaker`, `CircuitBreakerHandle::restart`).

- **ice: `ConsentResponseWait`, how long a consent request waits for its response**
  (`conf/ice-26-consent-late-responses`): `AgentConfig::consent_response_wait`,
  `SettingEngineBuilder::with_ice_consent_response_wait`. `Rto` (the default) is RFC 7675
  section 5.1's wait based on the round-trip time (see "Fixed"); `Fixed(duration)` is a fixed
  wait. A governed behaviour, `ice.consent-response-wait`: `BehaviourProfile::Chrome` takes
  `Fixed(60 s)`, libwebrtc's `kConnectionResponseTimeout` ("in some networks (2G), we observe
  up to 60s RTTs", `p2p/base/p2p_constants.h` @ a222406d), which takes an answer however far
  the round trip jumped; `Rfc`, `StrictRfc` and `Performance` keep `Rto`. Test:
  `agent_consent_delay_test.rs::test_a_response_after_its_wait_renews_nothing_unless_the_wait_is_fixed`,
  `test_no_consent_transaction_is_kept_past_the_consent_expiry`.
- **DTLS session resumption between a connection's transports, opt-in** (RFC 5764 section 3
  SHOULD, "as an optimization"; `conf/dtls-resume-3`, after two security reviews of
  `conf/dtls-resume-1` and `-2`): `SettingEngineBuilder::with_dtls_session_resumption(true)`.
  **Off by default, a standing departure from that SHOULD** (`docs/conformance.md`, "Standing
  departures from a SHOULD"; audit row RFC5764-3-4), because it is not free and most peers
  cannot take part. **What it costs**, measured with three unbundled transports on links with
  latency, time until every DTLS transport is connected: at a 100 ms round trip 453 ms off,
  753 ms on against a peer that issues no ticket (+300 ms, about 3 round trips: the others
  start one whole handshake later and resume nothing), 703 ms on between two engines with
  tickets (+250 ms, about 2.5 round trips); at 300 ms 1.353 s, 2.253 s (+900 ms) and 2.103 s
  (+750 ms). One datagram lost on the first handshake delays every transport, not one. What
  it saves is one signature and one verification per other transport. **No browser can take
  part**: libwebrtc sets `SSL_OP_NO_TICKET` (and has an `SSL_CTX` per transport), Firefox's
  `TransportLayerDtls::Setup()` turns session tickets and the session cache off; against a
  browser the setting only adds the wait. **With BUNDLE (one transport) it does nothing.**
  When the negotiation that sets up the transports sets up more than one in a DTLS
  role, the first client transport runs a full handshake and the others resume with the
  peer's **DTLS 1.3** tickets (`psk_dhe_ke` only, a fresh (EC)DHE exchange); server
  transports share the connection's ticket keys for their first handshake only. **No DTLS 1.2
  session id or ticket is asked for, issued or accepted by the peer connection in any
  configuration** (a DTLS 1.2 ticket carries the master secret, and a resumed 1.2 association
  runs no key exchange). The wait is bounded: a transport waits for the first handshake at
  most three of its initial flight intervals (1.2 s at 400 ms; 4.5 round trips where ICE
  measured one) and never more than 3 s (`LEADER_WAIT_MAX`: the ICE figure is one sample,
  which a slow-answering peer could stretch), not at all once the first failed, was closed or
  could not start, and not for a ticket that does not come: against a peer that issues none
  the others start as soon as the first handshake is complete (which is the cost above). The
  first reviewed form waited without bound for a stalled first handshake, and added 800 ms
  (two flight intervals) of waiting for a ticket against a peer without tickets; both are
  gone. A bundled connection asks for and issues no ticket (the same DTLS datagrams as
  without the setting); a transport added later, re-keying and a server's later handshake on
  the same transport are full handshakes; same remote fingerprints only, and each section's
  fingerprint check runs on the certificates stored with the ticket; client tickets are kept at
  most five minutes and dropped once every transport has started, and `close()` wipes the
  tickets left and the server side's ticket keys (new `session::SessionTicketIssuer::retire`
  / `is_retired` in `rtci-dtls`), not only the drop of the connection. RFC5764-3-4 is
  `partial` (implemented, not the default). New in `rtci-dtls`: `ConfigBuilder::with_dtls12_resumption`
  (DTLS 1.2 out of resumption, DTLS 1.3 kept), `ConfigBuilder::with_session_ticket_issuer`
  and `session::SessionTicketIssuer` (ticket keys shared by several configurations),
  `Tls13Session::peer_certificates` / `limit_lifetime`, `Dtls12Session::peer_certificates`,
  `HandshakeConfig::supports_dtls13` (now public). Tests: `tests/multi_transport_rtc2rtc.rs`
  (`unbundled_transports_wait_for_the_first_and_resume_its_dtls_session`,
  `a_first_handshake_that_never_completes_holds_the_others_back_three_flight_intervals_at_most`,
  `the_others_do_not_wait_for_a_ticket_that_does_not_come`,
  `the_session_costs_the_other_transports_the_first_handshake_on_links_with_latency`,
  `a_datagram_lost_on_the_first_handshake_delays_every_transport_with_the_session_on`,
  `a_first_handshake_that_never_completes_costs_the_others_the_bounded_wait_on_links_with_latency`,
  `a_final_answer_naming_another_certificate_is_checked_by_a_full_handshake_as_the_dtls_client`
  and `_as_the_dtls_server`,
  `by_default_a_final_answer_with_other_fingerprints_is_refused_with_the_session_made`,
  `with_dtls12_the_transports_neither_wait_nor_ask_for_a_ticket`,
  `a_bundled_connection_exchanges_no_ticket_with_the_session_on`,
  `a_transport_added_by_a_later_negotiation_runs_a_full_handshake`, the wrong-fingerprint and
  re-key tests); `transport/dtls/resumption.rs` (the re-check behind the admission gate in
  both roles, a final answer with other fingerprints, the store's lifetime and emptying, its
  filter on tickets without certificates, the wipe at close, the wait rules);
  `handler/dtls.rs` (the bound and its cap,
  `the_wait_for_the_leader_is_capped_whatever_round_trip_ice_measured`, a leader that cannot
  start, no resumption of a later handshake in place); `transport_close_test.rs`
  (`closing_the_connection_wipes_its_dtls_session`); `rtci-dtls` server-side re-check tests in DTLS 1.3 and 1.2
  (`the_server_runs_its_peer_certificate_check_again_on_a_resumed_client`).

- **mDNS may leave two kinds of host address unwrapped, each an opt-in setting, off by default
  (mdns-5; MDNSICE-3.1.2.2-4, -3.1.2.2-5, -3.1.2.3-1).** Only in `QueryAndGather`; in every
  behaviour profile off; neither ever unwraps an address `ice::mdns::is_global_unicast`
  refuses (private, loopback, link-local, unique-local `fc00::/7`, CGNAT `100.64.0.0/10`,
  documentation, IPv4-mapped, NAT64, ...), whatever a STUN server answered or the application
  marked.
  - `SettingEngineBuilder::with_multicast_dns_expose_known_public_addresses(true)`
    (`AgentConfig::multicast_dns_expose_known_public_addresses`), draft section 3.1.2.2: an
    address is shown public when a server-reflexive candidate's address is its base's ("the
    STUN response returns the same value as the local IP address") and the base is one of the
    transport's own host candidates. The gathering that shows it is unchanged (the `.local`
    candidate first, then the server-reflexive one, raddr `0.0.0.0` rport 9); host candidates
    of the next ICE generation carry the address ("skip mDNS protection for that address in
    future ICE gathering phases"), kept candidates included, as long as each restart's
    gathering shows it again. Per agent; `Agent::set_ice_servers` (called by
    `RTCPeerConnection::set_configuration`) discards it when the set of STUN / TURN servers
    changes (the section's SHOULD). The evidence is the server-reflexive candidate equal to
    its base, which `QueryAndGather` now always provides (see "Behaviour changes").
  - `SettingEngineBuilder::with_multicast_dns_expose_temporary_ipv6_addresses(true)`
    (`AgentConfig::multicast_dns_expose_temporary_ipv6_addresses`), draft section 3.1.2.3:
    the addresses the application marks as RFC 4941 temporary
    (`RTCPeerConnection::set_temporary_ipv6_addresses`, `Agent::set_temporary_ipv6_addresses`)
    go out as they are; an unmarked address stays hidden. `rtci-shared` has
    `ifaces::temporary_ipv6_addresses()` (Linux / Android `/proc/net/if_inet6`
    `IFA_F_TEMPORARY`; macOS / iOS `SIOCGIFAFLAG_IN6` `IN6_IFF_TEMPORARY`, not observed on a
    runner; Windows and elsewhere `Unsupported`: on Windows no flag has been shown to tell a
    temporary address from the stable one, so the setting has no effect there), and
    `rtci-stream-driver`'s `PeerDriver` marks its addresses from it at each gathering.

  What each exposes, and to whom: the first, an address the remote peer and the application
  (a web page, in a browser) already received as the server-reflexive candidate, now also
  as the host's own interface address; the second, the temporary address, to the same two,
  for its lifetime. Tests: `rtci-ice/src/agent/agent_mdns_exposure_test.rs`,
  `rtci-ice/src/mdns/mdns_exposure_test.rs`, `tests/ice_mdns_exposure.rs`,
  `stream-driver/tests/mdns_temporary.rs` (Linux, a temporary address made as root).

- **mDNS host candidates can fail closed (mdns-4, MDNSICE-3.1.1-6).** With mDNS
  `QueryAndGather`, a host candidate whose name cannot be registered (the application has no
  mDNS socket for its address family, or the agent holds the most names it can, 64) goes out,
  by default, under a `.local` name that is not published: draft-ietf-mmusic-mdns-ice-candidates
  section 3.1.1, "the ICE agent SHOULD still provide mDNS candidates in step 6 even if the
  local network does not support mDNS or mDNS registration fails in step 4".
  `SettingEngineBuilder::with_multicast_dns_fail_closed(true)` (`AgentConfig::multicast_dns_fail_closed`)
  provides no host candidate for such an address instead, UDP or TCP, for an embedder that
  must never offer a candidate its peer cannot resolve; its server-reflexive candidates are
  still gathered (raddr `0.0.0.0` rport 9). The literal address is written in neither case.
  An application with sockets of its own says which families it can send mDNS on with
  `RTCPeerConnection::set_multicast_dns_publishing(MulticastDnsPublishing { ipv4, ipv6 })`
  (`Agent::set_multicast_dns_publishing`) before it adds host candidates;
  `RTCPeerConnection::multicast_dns_mode` reads the mode; `Agent::multicast_dns_withholds`
  says whether an address's host candidates were withheld. `rtci-stream-driver`'s
  `PeerDriver` does it by itself, and `PeerDriverConfig::mdns_sockets` (`true` by default)
  turns its mDNS sockets off.
- **fec** (fec-15): libwebrtc's ULPFEC form for the pacer-written extensions, a `Chrome`
  profile row (`fec.ulpfec-zero-mutable-extensions`, `DefaultInterceptorOptions::ulpfec_zero_mutable_extensions`):
  `UlpfecSendBuilder::with_mutable_extensions_zeroed` protects the transport-wide sequence
  number, abs-send-time and toffset values as zeros (libwebrtc computes its FEC before it
  writes them, `RtpSenderEgress::SendPacket` @ a222406d) and
  `UlpfecReceiveBuilder::with_mutable_extensions_zeroed` zeroes them in the decoder's copies
  (`ZeroMutableExtensions`), so a packet rebuilt on either side is exact with those values
  zero. `configure_video_red_ulpfec_with(registry, media_engine, zero)`; the `Chrome` profile's
  chain has it on. `Rfc` keeps RFC 5109 section 8's FEC over the packet as sent.

- **fec** (fec-13): RFC 8854 section 5.2's `video/flexfec` in the offer as a setting:
  `DefaultInterceptorOptions::video_flexfec` / `configure_video_flexfec` registers
  `video/flexfec` (payload type 49, `repair-window=10000000`) and runs the RFC 8627 coder in the
  standard chain at slots of its own (`FLEXFEC_ENCODER_SLOT` 5_100, `FLEXFEC_WIRE_IMAGE_SLOT`
  1_510, `FLEXFEC_DECODER_SLOT` 10_310), beside ULPFEC's, so a chain can run both. On in the
  `StrictRfc` profile (row `fec.video-flexfec`); off by default and in `Chrome`, because RFC 8627
  section 1.1.7 has an answerer offered FlexFEC and RTX answer with FlexFEC only, which would
  leave two default peers without RTX (audit row RFC8854-5.2-1, `conflict`). No change to the
  default's offers.

- **ULPFEC across an SRTP key change** (RFC 5109 section 11, row RFC5109-11-3 untested ->
  tested): `tests/ulpfec_across_srtp_rekeying_rtc2rtc.rs` sends a FEC block whose first media
  packet leaves under one DTLS association's keys and whose second media packet and FEC
  packet leave under a new association's (`renew_dtls_association`), after the receiver
  dropped the old keys; whichever media packet the network loses is rebuilt. No engine
  change.
- **Browser cell: the engine's ULPFEC in RED rebuilt by the browser.** `scenarios.spec.mjs`
  has Rust send VP8 in RED with ULPFEC (the `Chrome` profile's form), NACK off on both sides,
  and checks that the browser decodes every frame although Rust's sender discarded every
  tenth media packet after the FEC protected it (`examples/interop-peer`
  `?drop_video_every=N`, reported as `videoDropped`). The earlier finding that Chromium does
  not rebuild from the engine's FEC was wrong: the packets are byte for byte what libwebrtc's
  `UlpfecReceiver` reads, and Chromium rebuilds from them; the earlier cell's threshold under
  random netem loss failed on frames whose media and FEC packets were both dropped (VP8
  without NACK then waits for a key frame). The browser offers VP8, red and ulpfec only
  (`setCodecPreferences`): as offerer Firefox otherwise also receives the VP9 and AV1 it
  offered, with its default NACK, and turns NACK on for the whole receive stream. Firefox
  rebuilds every dropped packet too; it never decodes the fixture's first group of pictures in
  that cell, loss or not, which its column leaves out. No engine change.
- **FlexFEC-03 repair packets within the path MTU** (draft-ietf-payload-flexible-fec-scheme-03
  section 6.2): `FlexFec03Encoder` builds no repair packet larger than
  `FLEXFEC03_MAX_REPAIR_PACKET_SIZE` (1436 octets: a 1500-octet path under IPv6, UDP and a
  16-octet SRTP tag; `with_max_packet_size` sets another); the block goes without it and the
  repair stream's sequence numbers skip nothing. Engine behaviour change only for media
  packets above about 1400 octets.
- **RFC 8854 audit** (`docs/conformance/audit/rfc8854.md`): 23 rows (MUST 3 tested, 1 n/a;
  SHOULD 6 tested, 6 partial, 2 missing, 3 n/a; MAY 1 tested, 1 missing), and a test that no
  behaviour profile offers a FEC-only m= section (section 5.2).
- **Browser cell: video RED + ULPFEC from the browser.** `examples/interop-peer` takes
  `?video_red_ulpfec=1` (`DefaultInterceptorOptions::video_red_ulpfec`) and reports the
  engine's FEC counts (`fec`); `scenarios.spec.mjs` has the browser send VP8 in RED with
  ULPFEC, NACK off, through netem loss, and checks that the engine rebuilt packets from it.
  `scripts/test-env/hosted-cell.sh` runs a browser cell on a disposable Linux machine (a
  GitHub-hosted runner through `agent-test.yml`) outside the test image.
- **Video `red` + `ulpfec` in the `Chrome` behaviour profile.**
  `DefaultInterceptorOptions::video_red_ulpfec` (profile row `fec.video-red-ulpfec`: `Rfc`
  `false`, `Chrome` `true`): `register_default_interceptors` then registers `video/red` (116),
  RTX for it (117, `apt=116`) and `video/ulpfec` (43) after the video codecs, as Chromium
  offers them (libwebrtc `GetDefaultSupportedFormats`), and `configure_video_red_ulpfec`
  installs ULPFEC in RED in both directions (FEC in RED packets of its own, read from the wire
  tap, loss-driven amount). The default stays RFC 8854 section 7's: neither is offered for
  video. `UlpfecReceiveInterceptor` now reads RED and FEC under the payload types the stream's
  section negotiated (as the sender already did), not only the builder's: an answer keeps
  the offerer's numbers. Engine behaviour change for the `Chrome` profile (its video offers
  and chain).
- **FEC statistics.** The receiver's webrtc-stats now count all the FEC received for a
  stream (8.5): `fecPacketsReceived` and `fecBytesReceived` include the FEC blocks of the
  stream's RED packets (RFC 5109 section 14.2) and the packets of a FEC session of its own
  (section 14.1; those also count in `packetsReceived` / `bytesReceived`, webrtc-stats 7.1),
  besides a FEC SSRC's; `fecPacketsDiscarded` is measured for ULPFEC (FEC whose packets all
  arrived or were rebuilt, FEC the recovery window left behind or that arrived outside it,
  malformed FEC). `RTCPeerConnection::fec_stats()` (`FecStats`, `FecSentStats`,
  `FecReceivedStats`) has what webrtc-stats has no member for: the FEC each outbound stream
  sent (packets and payload octets, any carriage, ULPFEC and FlexFEC), the media packets FEC
  rebuilt, and the discards by reason. In the interceptor crate: `UlpfecDecoderStats` gains
  `discarded_unneeded`, `discarded_expired` and `discarded()`; `UlpfecReceiveInterceptor`
  passes `UlpfecReceiveStats` application-ward on an empty RTCP carrier when its counts change
  (and `receive_stats(ssrc)`); every packet a ULPFEC or FlexFEC encoder puts FEC into carries
  a `FecSent` mark. An application that drives a chain itself sees the carriers (empty RTCP
  packets with that attribute) on the read leg.
- **data channel** (up-340, test only): `tests/data_channel_close_sibling_rtc2rtc.rs` holds the
  reproduction of webrtc-rs/rtc#340 by @schiapellone. A channel closed by the receiver while
  the peer still sends on it, beside a healthy channel, used to make the read of its stream
  fail mid-pass and drop the messages already read from the other streams in that pass
  (acknowledged, so lost for good). The fork had the fix without a test: b91196d7 (the read of
  a closed stream ends its data, not the pass) and e9b19fa3 (a stream the application stopped
  reading drops what arrives on it). No behaviour change.
- **rtp** (up-336): the H.264 / H.265 Annex B splitter (`annex_b_nal_units`, used by
  `H264Payloader` and `HevcPayloader`) finds start codes with `memchr::memmem` instead of a byte
  at a time; the NAL units are the same (test
  `h264_test::annex_b_nal_units_are_those_a_byte_scan_finds`). Measured on a GitHub-hosted
  ubuntu runner, release build, best of 15: a 30 KB one-slice frame 14.0 us to 0.57 us, a 1 MB
  eight-slice frame 500 us to 27 us, SPS + PPS + a 100 B slice 106 ns to 92 ns; 1000 NAL units
  of 5 B each 19.8 us to 21.5 us (+8%). Same change as webrtc-rs/rtc#336 by @g4lb.
- **tooling** (up-watch): `scripts/upstream-watch.py` lists what webrtc-rs did since the fork last
  looked: `webrtc-rs/rtc` commits after the merged one, its pull requests and issues opened or
  updated since the triage day, and `webrtc-rs/webrtc` commits (`master`, `v0.17.x`). Both
  points are FORK.md's (new row "Open upstream work last triaged"). Read-only GitHub API
  calls; no workflow runs it.
- **`SettingEngineBuilder::with_dtls_session_resumption(bool)`** (default `false`): with
  `true` the transports of a connection's unbundled sections share one DTLS session (RFC 5764
  section 3; see the entry "DTLS session resumption between a connection's transports,
  opt-in" for what it costs); `false`, the default, gives every association a full handshake
  at once, as before.
- **rtci-dtls**: `session::SessionTicketIssuer` and `ConfigBuilder::with_session_ticket_issuer`:
  ticket keys (and the record of used tickets) several configurations share, so that a ticket
  one issued is accepted, once, by another; `SessionTicketIssuer::retire` wipes the keys
  (zeroized) before the last holder is dropped, after which no ticket is issued or accepted.
  `Tls13Session::peer_certificates` and `Dtls12Session::peer_certificates`.
- **rtci-dtls** (documentation): what DTLS 1.2 session resumption costs is stated on
  `ConfigBuilder`, `with_session_tickets`, `with_session_store`, `with_session_cache`,
  `with_dtls12_resumption`, the `session` module and the crate: a resumed DTLS 1.2
  association runs no key exchange and an RFC 5077 ticket is the master secret sealed under
  the server's ticket key, so there is no forward secrecy against the ticket key, the session
  cache or the client's store; DTLS 1.3 resumption (`psk_dhe_ke`) keeps it. The stand-alone
  default is unchanged: once tickets, a cache or a store are configured both versions resume
  unless `with_dtls12_resumption(false)`.
- **turn** (`conf/transport3-mays`): `ClientConfig::software_in_indications` puts the
  client's SOFTWARE in its Send indications too (RFC 8489 section 6.1: "Indications MAY include
  a SOFTWARE attribute"). Off by default, so nothing changes on the wire: Send indications are
  the relayed data path. Test: `rtci-turn`
  `client_software_mtu_test.rs::test_send_indications_carry_software_only_when_configured`.
  RFC8489-6.1-3 is `tested`.
- **ice** (`conf/transport3-mays`): `AgentConfig::new_tie_breaker_on_restart` and
  `SettingEngineBuilder::with_ice_new_tie_breaker_on_restart` draw a new tiebreaker at each
  ICE restart (RFC 8445 section 16.1: "The agent MAY change the number when an ICE restart
  occurs"); a restart that is rolled back gives the old one back. Off by default: the
  tiebreaker stays for the agent's life, as before and as in libwebrtc. Test: `rtci-ice`
  `agent_rfc8445_test.rs::test_ice_restart_draws_a_new_tie_breaker_only_when_configured`.
  RFC8445-16.1-4 is `tested`.
- **An embedder address policy for ICE, both directions** (`conf/ice-24-address-policy`):
  `SettingEngineBuilder::with_ice_address_policy(IceAddressPolicy)` (and
  `AgentConfig::address_policy` for the agent alone). One predicate over a `SocketAddr`, an
  `AddressDirection` (inbound / outbound) and an `AddressPurpose` (`RemoteCandidate`,
  `PeerReflexiveSource`, `StunTurnServer`, `InboundDatagramSource`), asked wherever an address
  enters the ICE agent or the peer connection: a datagram (direct, relayed by the engine's TURN
  allocation, or ICE-TCP stream data) from a refused source is dropped before the agent, DTLS
  or the media read it (no STUN response, no peer-reflexive candidate, no consent, no pair, no
  data accepted: agent `handle_read`, `data_path`, `is_valid_non_stun_traffic`; peer connection
  `read_on_transport`); an ICE-TCP connection from it is refused (`handle_stream_accepted`) and
  one that turns refused is reset (`handle_stream_read`); a TURN TCP peer connection from it is
  not bound; a refused remote candidate (signalled, or an mDNS name's address) is never held or
  paired, and `add_remote_candidate` treats it as W3C webrtc-pc 4.4.2 "administratively
  prohibited"; a refused peer-reflexive source is not learned (RFC 8445 7.3.1.3) and so not
  answered, a request that arrives before the peer's credentials included (RFC 8445 7.3: it
  was answered at once, with only the destination policy asked; `conf/ice-24r-address-policy`);
  a remote TCP candidate on a refused address gets no permission on the engine's TURN TCP
  allocation (RFC 6062 5.3); a STUN or TURN server address the policy refuses, after its name resolved, is never
  sent anything (skipped as a failed address). The predicate sees IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses
  as IPv4. With the "relay" ICE transport policy and a policy refusing private peers, no
  datagram leaves from or goes to a host address and none is signalled. The default allows
  everything and asks nothing: engine behaviour is unchanged without it.
  `with_remote_address_filter` is kept as it was (it refuses remote candidates and
  peer-reflexive sources only) and composes with the policy. Tests:
  `rtci-ice` `address_policy_test.rs` (six), `tests/ice_address_policy.rs` (seven),
  `tests/turn_tcp_relay.rs` (two). The two-peer tests draw the engine's random numbers from a
  seed and carry what a peer writes before time moves on: as first written, their loop
  delivered the answer to a consent request (RFC 7675) only after the next timer, often the
  requester's own end of the transaction, and the answerer then left the connected state on
  54 of 200 seeds, with or without a policy. Audit:
  RFC8828-5.2-P5 is a new `tested` control row; notes on WEBRTC-4.4.1.4-4 and RFC8445-7.3.1.3-1.

- **ULPFEC in an RTP session of its own, in the chain (RFC 5109 sections 7.2, 14.1).**
  `StreamInfo::fec_session` (`FecSessionStream`: the SSRC the FEC stream has inside the chain,
  the payload type of `ulpfec` in the FEC session's m= section, `onelevelonly`) says that a
  stream's FEC runs in a second RTP session. `UlpfecSendInterceptor` then sends the stream's
  FEC as a stream of its own under that SSRC and `UlpfecReceiveInterceptor` reads it there,
  whatever carriage the builder names and whatever the media section lists (section 14: the
  multiplexing is "indicated out of band"); the media stream is left as it is, not wrapped in
  RED. `FecSessionSsrcMap` is the boundary between the chain, which keys what it keeps on the
  SSRC, and the FEC session's transport, where "the SSRC value SHALL be the same as the SSRC
  value of the media stream it protects": every SSRC of the session's RTP and RTCP is the wire
  SSRC XOR one key, in both directions, with no table. A packet the FEC of another transport
  rebuilt is delivered with the media stream's transport context. **Breaking**: `StreamInfo`
  has a new public field (`..Default::default()` in a struct literal covers it).
- **ULPFEC as a separate stream: a FEC session of its own (RFC 5109 sections 7.2, 14.1,
  14.3).** `RTCPeerConnection::add_fec_session(transceiver, semantics)` offers, for the media
  of one transceiver, a second m= section that lists only `ulpfec` (one dynamic payload type,
  the media's rate), outside the BUNDLE group and so on a transport of its own (its own
  candidates, DTLS association and SRTP keys), grouped with the media section by
  `a=group:FEC-FR <media> <fec>` (RFC 5956 section 4.1, the default) or `a=group:FEC ...`
  (RFC 4756, the semantics RFC 5109 names; `RTCFecGroupSemantics`). The returned transceiver is
  the session: it has a mid, a direction, can be stopped, and never has a track
  (`fec_session_of`, `fec_session_protects`). Once the answer keeps the section and repeats
  the grouping, the ULPFEC of the protected sender's streams travels there, each FEC stream
  with the SSRC of the media stream it protects, marker 0, sequence numbers of its own and
  RTCP of its own; what arrives there repairs the protected receiver's streams and is never
  delivered as media. `SettingEngineBuilder::with_separate_fec_sessions(true)` accepts an
  offered FEC session (same grouping and payload type in the answer, the direction of the
  transceiver it protects). `configure_ulpfec_sessions` adds the interceptors (encoder with
  its wire tap, decoder); the amount of FEC follows the reported loss and comes out of the
  target the application encodes at. In the interceptor crate: `FecSessionPacket` marks what
  was read in a FEC session for the decoder, and `UlpfecReceiveBuilder::sessions()` keeps a
  decoder for each bound stream.
  **Defaults are unchanged**: nothing offers a FEC session by itself, and an offered one is
  refused (port 0, the group left out), as RFC 8854 section 5.2 asks of a WebRTC endpoint
  ("SHOULD NOT be offered"; "Answerers SHOULD reject any FEC-only "m=" lines, unless they
  specifically know how to handle such a thing"). No browser accepts one.
  **Known limits**: the FEC section negotiates no header extension, so the FEC session's
  congestion controller has no per-packet feedback and stays at its start estimate; FEC for a
  stream whose SSRC the description does not declare is used from that stream's first media
  packet on.

### Fixed

- **ICE: a peer that can only reach us by its own checks is not failed at end-of-candidates**
  (ice-27, reported by a consumer's ICE-TCP tests). Since the RFC 8445 checklist (first
  released in 0.1.0 and v0.22.0+brainwires.6), an agent failed at once when both sides had
  signalled end-of-candidates and its checklist had no pair. Two kinds of peer have no pair
  until their own check arrives: one whose only candidates are `tcptype active` (it dials our
  passive TCP candidate; the agent pairs nothing with an active candidate) and one whose only
  candidates are `.local` names the agent does not resolve (mDNS off, or the query timed
  out). Against either the connection failed before the peer's first check could arrive, so
  a peer that could only dial our passive ICE-TCP candidate never connected once both sides
  sent `a=end-of-candidates`. Now the agent notes such signalled candidates, and while one of
  them can reach a local candidate (an active one, a local passive TCP candidate of its
  family; a `.local` name, a local candidate of its transport) the checklist stays Running
  (RFC 8838 section 8: "MUST keep each checklist in the Running state as long as it expects
  candidate pairs to be incrementally added"): the peer's check forms the peer-reflexive pair
  and the agent connects, and if no check comes the checking timeout fails it as before
  (`disconnected_timeout + failed_timeout`, 30 s by default). The peer connection now hands
  remote active candidates to the agent instead of dropping them itself, and no longer takes
  an active candidate for administratively prohibited because of its port: RFC 6544 section
  4.5 sets that port to 9, a Fetch bad port, but no connection is ever made to it (the W3C
  rule prohibits connections to bad ports). A checklist with no
  remote candidate at all, or whose pairs have all failed with nothing that could still dial
  in, fails at once as before. Tests: `agent_checklist_test.rs::
  a_peer_reached_only_by_its_own_checks_keeps_the_empty_checklist_running_and_connects`,
  `a_peer_reached_only_by_its_own_checks_that_never_checks_fails_by_the_timeout`,
  `an_active_tcp_candidate_with_nothing_of_ours_to_dial_fails_the_empty_checklist_at_once`,
  `an_ice_restart_forgets_the_candidates_that_could_only_dial_us`, `tests/ice_tcp_active_passive.rs::
  test_ice_tcp_passive_side_connects_when_the_peer_signals_only_active_and_end_of_candidates`.
- **congestion control: packets sent before a new path carried anything are not the new
  path's loss.** At a path change (the peer connection's `PathChanged`, or packets from new
  addresses) the estimate starts over and the packets sent into the path that was left are
  forgotten. The two ends do not take the new path into use at the same instant, though: what
  an endpoint sends between its own change and the moment the path carries media to the other
  end goes nowhere, and those packets were reported as the new path's loss. With bandwidth
  probing on, a probe cluster asked for at the instant of the change (23 padding packets in
  a chain without a pacer) is among them: after an ICE restart whose controlled side learned
  of the pair 10 ms before the controlling side, 24 of the first 47 packets it sent were
  counted lost and the estimate that had just started over at 300 kbit/s was cut to 298.9
  (`tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs::
  an_estimate_started_over_on_a_new_path_does_not_fall_without_evidence`, which only held
  while retransmissions of old packets watered the fraction down to under 10 %). Now a packet
  sent on a new path earlier than every packet reported received over it, and reported as
  not received, is released without a verdict (the send history, `before_the_path_carried`),
  as the packets of the old path are; a packet lost after one that arrived is a loss as
  ever. Tests: `rtpfb::history::tests::
  a_loss_before_anything_arrived_on_a_new_path_is_not_reported`,
  `a_loss_before_the_first_arrival_of_a_call_is_reported`, `gcc::twcc_gcc::tests::
  packets_sent_before_a_new_path_carried_anything_are_not_its_loss`.
- **without a retransmission format, a NACK was never answered on the wire with the default
  interceptors** (nortx-1). When no `rtx` format is negotiated (a peer that does not support
  RFC 4588, an application that registers none) the NACK responder answers a request with
  the packet again as it was sent: the media SSRC, the same sequence number, and so the SRTP
  packet index of the first transmission. A packet index protects one packet (RFC 3711
  section 3.3.1; RFC 7714 section 8.1): the SRTP sender protects the same packet again and
  refuses a different one. The default set stamps the abs-send-time extension (offered on
  video since it joined the default set) and, where negotiated, the RFC 6051 timestamp,
  wire-ward of the responder, at the instant a packet leaves: the retransmission got a new
  stamp, was a different packet under a used index, and was dropped below the interceptors
  (`unsent_index_reused`), silently. No lost packet was repaired (a receiver waited for a
  key frame), while the responder had lowered the media target to make room for each
  retransmission (RFC 4588 section 7) and the congestion controller had recorded each as
  sent. Both stampers now give a packet that passes again, marked a retransmission under an
  SSRC and sequence number they have seen, what its first transmission left with (the stamp,
  or no timestamp), as the TWCC sender already kept its transport-wide number: the packet
  reaches the SRTP sender byte for byte as it first left. An RTX retransmission is a new
  packet and is stamped as it passes, as before. Also in 0.1.0. Not affected: a stream with
  RTX (every default codec has it), and a chain without those stampers. Tests
  `tests/nack_without_rtx_rtc2rtc.rs::a_lost_packet_is_sent_again_as_it_was_and_arrives_when_no_rtx_is_negotiated`,
  `a_packet_sent_again_as_it_was_keeps_its_abs_send_time`,
  `a_packet_sent_again_as_it_was_leaves_as_its_first_transmission_did`.
- **video sent as RED was never repaired by retransmission** (red-2; the `Chrome` profile's
  `fec.video-red-ulpfec`). Two defects, either of which made every retransmission of a RED
  packet useless:
  - The NACK responder sent every retransmission of a stream under the one RTX payload type
    of the format the stream was bound with. RFC 4588 section 8.1 ties a retransmission
    format to one original payload type (`apt`: "the payload type of the associated original
    stream"), and a receiver restores the payload type from the `apt` of the format the
    retransmission arrives under: a RED packet (payload type 116) retransmitted under the
    RTX of VP8 (97, `apt=96`) came back as VP8 with the RED header in front of it (traced
    call: 87 retransmissions, none usable). The responder now takes the RTX format whose
    `apt` is the payload type the packet left under, among the formats of the stream's
    section and the stream's own pair, as libwebrtc does (`rtp_sender.cc`, `BuildRtxPacket`).
    A packet whose payload type has no RTX format, on a stream that negotiated RTX, is not
    retransmitted at all (libwebrtc sends nothing either): never as a second copy on the
    media SSRC. A stream that negotiated no RTX is repaired with the packet again as it was
    sent, as before. This also holds for a source that switches between the formats of its
    section (RFC 7160): each packet goes under its own format's RTX.
  - An offerer dropped `rtx apt=<red>` when it applied the answer: entering the answer's
    formats under its own payload type numbers counted only media and FEC formats as the
    primary of an RTX format, so the RTX of a RED format was left out of the negotiated list,
    and the offerer could neither send nor read a retransmitted RED packet (between two
    engines only the answerer's direction had the format).
  - The FEC data of a FEC packet in RED (ULPFEC in a RED packet of its own, in the media's
    sequence space) is not retransmitted when the packet is asked for: the media's own
    retransmission answers the loss. Its sequence number is answered, with three octets
    under the RTX of `red`: the original sequence number and the RED block header. A
    receiver that puts frames together in sequence-number order cannot tell a lost FEC
    packet from a lost one-packet frame, and would wait for it and ask for a key frame;
    restored, the answer is a FEC packet with nothing in it, which reaches the application
    as any FEC packet does, without a payload. libwebrtc keeps no FEC packet for
    retransmission (`ulpfec_generator.cc:233`, `set_allow_retransmission(false)`) and
    ignores a NACK for one (`rtp_sender.cc:348-351`); its receiver finds frames without the
    number. Without an RTX stream a FEC packet is not sent again.

  Tests `rtci-interceptor/tests/nack_rtx_red.rs`,
  `in_the_chrome_profile_a_lost_red_packet_is_retransmitted_under_the_rtx_of_red`,
  `an_rtx_format_whose_primary_is_a_red_format_is_numbered_with_it`. Not affected: streams
  not sent in RED with one media format (the default profile).

- **media** (`conf/red-3-fec-sequence-holes`): `SampleBuilder` gave a sample a duration of
  zero when the packet that follows it had the last sequence number before the wrap (65535):
  the search for the next packet's timestamp ran over a range that does not wrap. It walks
  the sequence numbers as they wrap now.
- **a stream received as RED had no RTCP feedback: with video RED / ULPFEC (the `Chrome`
  profile) two engines never raised their send rate** (red-1). A receiver learns a
  stream's format from the payload type of its first packet; when that is the `red` format
  (RFC 2198), which is described without `a=rtcp-fb` lines, the stream was bound to the
  interceptors with no feedback at all, while the sender, which knows the stream by its
  media codec, expected the feedback negotiated for that codec. With RFC 8888 congestion
  control feedback (`ack ccfb`, what two engines negotiate) the receiver therefore reported
  the audio stream only: the sender's congestion controller saw a path that carried 50
  kbit/s, its estimate stopped at the first step above the start value (315 kbit/s) and
  after a capacity collapse stayed at the floor; NACK and key frame requests about the video
  were not bound either. A stream bound under `red` now has the feedback of the format it
  carries (the one its fmtp names, else the section's first media format) beside any of its
  own, as libwebrtc configures a stream from its first media codec whatever payload type
  arrives. Found with the capacity instrument's `chrome` chain (send target 90 kbit/s for
  the whole call); the row at fault was `fec.video-red-ulpfec`, alone. Not affected: the
  default profile (no video RED), and a peer whose feedback is transport-wide (bound by
  the header extension: Chromium). Test `a_red_stream_has_the_feedback_of_the_format_it_carries`.
  Still open after this entry: a RED packet retransmitted over RTX is not usable by the
  receiver (it leaves under the media format's RTX payload type); see red-2.

- **circuit breaker: a receiver that reports from several of its SSRCs is counted once**
  (rtcpbudget-4). RFC 8108 section 5.1 has every SSRC of an endpoint report on every stream
  it receives, so a peer that follows it (this engine with
  `rtcp_report_from_every_ssrc`, the `StrictRfc` profile) sends several report blocks about
  each flow in one compound packet, the same reception each time. The RFC 8083 breaker took
  each copy for a report of its own: the media timeout's count of reports without progress
  was reached in a fraction of the reporting intervals, a loss interval's packets were taken
  by the first copy and the others showed none, and the spacing between copies read as a
  reporting interval of zero. A flow now follows one reporting SSRC and takes another only
  once the one it follows has been silent for the RTCP timeout (the reporter left or changed
  its SSRC). With a peer that reports once (the default, libwebrtc) nothing changes. Tests
  `every_ssrc_of_the_receiver_reporting_counts_as_one_report`,
  `another_reporting_ssrc_is_followed_once_the_first_has_been_silent_for_the_rtcp_timeout`.
- **interceptor / pacer** (pacing-3): the deadline the pacer names is an instant at which the
  packet leaves, at every rate. Where a packet's wait is not a whole number of nanoseconds
  (12 000 bits at 840 kbit/s) the budget, refilled to the named instant, could be a fraction
  of a nanosecond's worth short: the packet stayed, and `poll_timeout` named the same instant
  again, so a driver that follows the deadlines exactly span (the test worlds hid it by
  pushing their clock on). The budget now covers a packet to within what the rate adds in
  two nanoseconds. `pacer::tests::a_packet_is_releasable_at_the_instant_named_for_it`,
  `pacer_deadline.rs::every_deadline_the_pacer_names_releases_a_packet_and_the_next_is_later`.
  Known effect, measured with the capacity instrument (1000 seeds each way, a capacity drop
  from 2.5 Mbit/s to 300 kbit/s behind a 300 ms drop-tail queue): with packets leaving at
  the named instants, a STUN consent datagram (RFC 7675) meets the full link queue in the
  overload after the drop in 30.6 % of calls instead of 25.2 %, and a peer reports
  `disconnected` for a moment in 17.4 % instead of 12.8 % (behind a 1000 ms queue 21.2 %
  instead of 14.0 % of 400). Most are the transient that one lost consent check gives (in that
  cell: median 0.5 s, longest 1.1 s of 1000 calls; no peer stayed disconnected, none failed),
  and the picture, audio and recovery figures do not move. Not every episode is that short:
  over the six paced cells of the instrument's record on the landing tree (train 34 round 1,
  629 calls with an episode, median 0.6 s) 10 calls had one longer than 2 s, the longest 6.58 s
  behind a 100 ms queue and 9.20 s with 5 % loss on the reverse path, where 2 of 200 calls were
  still outside `connected` at the end of the run; long single episodes and those 2 of 200 are
  there without this change too (5.92 s and 6.31 s the longest, 2 of 200). STUN does not pass
  the pacer; the drop is the link's.
- **Bandwidth probing in a chain without a pacer never got a result** (in 0.1.0 too). A probe
  cluster was measured on the packets the pacer marked as the cluster's; with the pacer taken
  out of the default interceptors (or in any chain built without one) nothing marked a packet,
  so the congestion controller asked for clusters, the NACK responder sent each one's padding
  as a burst, and no result ever came: the start-up clusters among them, so an open 2.5 Mbit/s
  path was reached at the 8% a second of draft-ietf-rmcat-gcc-02 section 5.5 (about 1.4 Mbit/s
  after 20 s from the 300 kbit/s start) instead of within a second (RFC 8836 section 2,
  requirement 4). Now the responder's padding carries the cluster's mark (`ProbePacket`) when no
  pacer took the request, and a cluster whose packets left in one instant is measured by how
  far apart the path delivered it (`burst_estimate`: the narrowest link's rate, never above the
  rate the cluster was asked for at). Where no cluster can be sent at all (no pacer and no RTX
  stream to pad on) the controller stops asking after the first cluster no packet left for,
  until another stream is bound or starts to send: a request that can have no result is not
  repeated. The start is now 1 Mbit/s after 0.37 s and the 2.5 Mbit/s maximum after 0.47 s
  in both chains without a pacer (`tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs::
  an_open_link_is_found_within_a_second_without_a_pacer`). A known limit of the burst
  measurement: a path that delivers a burst as one aggregate shows no spread and is credited
  with the rate asked for; the delay-based controller corrects it once the media follows
  (`burst_estimate`). Tests: `rtci-interceptor/tests/probe_without_pacer.rs`.

- **After an ICE restart onto a new path the default chain climbed at 8% a second** (in 0.1.0
  too): bandwidth probing was told nothing of a path change. The estimator starts over at its
  starting rate on a new selected pair (`PathChanged`, or
  `CongestionControlHandle::notify_path_change`), but the probe controller kept what it had
  noted of the old path. During an outage the estimator halves at every feedback timeout, and
  each halving is a "large drop" that the probe after a drop asks about a second later: the
  cluster for the rate before the last halving (133 kbit/s), asked into the dead path, still
