  awaited its result when the new pair was selected, held the controller's one slot through
  the half second in which a cluster for an application-limited sender would have been due,
  and no start-up cluster followed. On the capacity instrument's outage cell (a 4 s outage
  ended by an ICE restart, the new path open at 2.5 Mbit/s, 200 calls) the target was back at
  1 Mbit/s 15.1 s after the new pair and averaged 1504 kbit/s 15 to 25 s after it; with the
  probe after a drop turned off, 1.0 s in 134 of the 200 calls and 12 to 13 s in the others. Now a
  path change starts probing over as at the start of the call
  (`ProbeController::on_path_change`, new): the start-up clusters again, at three and six
  times the rate the estimator starts over at and on while the new path carries what is
  asked, and the target's recent high, the drop below it and the cluster awaiting its result
  are dropped with the old path (the fall to the starting rate is not a capacity drop).
  libwebrtc does the same (`GoogCcNetworkController::OnNetworkRouteChange`:
  `ProbeController::Reset`, then the exponential probes again). MEASURED on the same cell
  (200 calls, hosted runs 45609964155 against 45607015088): 1 Mbit/s 0.8 s after the new pair
  (1.02 s at most; no call slower) and the 2.5 Mbit/s maximum through the 15 to 25 s window;
  with a receiver that has no bound on a gap the first new picture comes 2.3 s earlier in two
  thirds of the calls (0.74 s after the new pair against 3.08 s on average). WHAT IT COSTS:
  with the reference receiver (a gap given up after 300 ms) the first new picture comes
  0.12 s later in those calls (0.70 s after the new pair against 0.58 s): the start-up
  clusters share the first moments of the new path with the key frame. The chains without a
  pacer were at 1 Mbit/s 0.5 s after the new pair before and are now (their probe after a
  drop is off, so no cluster was outstanding). The OTHER direction gains in every chain:
  the callee's target over the ten seconds after the new pair averages 1521 kbit/s against
  507 with the pacer, and 1345 to 1367 against 395 without one. There the callee, which
  selects the new pair 10 ms before the caller, loses its first cluster whole (nothing but
  STUN crosses until both have switched); it used to ask for that one cluster only, and now
  the next start-up cluster follows when the first is given up a second later. Every other
  cell of the instrument is unchanged (4600 calls in fifteen cells, 0 differ). Tests:
  `cc::probe::tests::a_path_change_starts_probing_over_and_forgets_the_drop`,
  `the_fall_to_the_starting_rate_at_a_path_change_is_not_a_drop`,
  `rtci-interceptor/tests/probing_across_a_path_change.rs`,
  `libwebrtcs_probe_after_a_drop_is_not_asked_across_a_path_change`,
  `tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs::an_ice_restart_onto_an_open_path_finds_its_rate_within_a_second_in_the_default_chain`,
  `::the_peer_that_selects_the_new_pair_first_finds_the_path_though_its_first_cluster_is_lost`.

- **interceptor / GCC** (collapse-1): over-use that lasts through several feedback reports
  while a probe's measurement is held no longer multiplies the estimate by 0.85 on every
  report. draft-ietf-rmcat-gcc-02 section 5.5 sets `A_hat(i) = beta * R_hat(i)`; the
  controller took the probe's measurement for what the path delivers whenever one was held
  (six seconds after any probe result), and from the second report of an over-use on that
  measurement was the estimate itself, so the estimate fell by 15% every 50 ms whatever
  arrived: 268 kbit/s to the 100 kbit/s floor in 0.3 s while 213 to 252 kbit/s was received
  (the path of `tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs`, where the estimate under a 300 kbit/s
  cap averaged 200 kbit/s and fell to the floor again and again). The measurement now stands
  in for the received rate only while the sender is received below it (application limited,
  as before); a sender received at the measurement or above it is cut to 0.85 times the
  received rate, and over-use never raises an estimate that rests on a probe.
  `rate_control::tests::lasting_over_use_with_a_probe_measurement_follows_the_received_rate`.
- **interceptor / bandwidth probing** (collapse-2): a probe cluster's padding belongs to the
  cluster. The NACK responder made a whole cluster of padding-only RTX packets for every
  `ProbeRequest`, and the pacer kept what did not leave in the cluster "until budget was
  spare". With a backlog in the pacer (after a capacity drop, during its pause) every cluster
  was filled by the backlog and its 22 padding packets stayed queued, for seconds: 191 of them
  after ten clusters in `tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs`. They left inside later
  clusters with the RTX sequence numbers they were given when made, far behind the stream's
  newest, where the receiver's replay protection and feedback window no longer take them; no
  report ever named them, so those clusters were never reported in full and gave no result
  (every cluster after the cap; an estimate at its floor with an application-limited sender
  then stayed there, 35 s on an open path in the cap matrix's seed 5 and 3 of 1000 seeds of
  the capacity review). Now the pacer says how much padding a cluster needs beyond the media
  it holds (`ProbeFill`, on the request's carrier), the responder makes that much (none while
  a backlog waits), and padding that could not leave in its cluster is discarded when the
  cluster ends (`PacerInterceptor::padding_discarded` counts it). The congestion controller
  counts in a cluster only the packets per-packet feedback will report (audio without
  feedback that left during a cluster was waited for and never came), and a cluster one of
  whose reports is still missing 500 ms after it left is measured on the others instead of
  being given up. `rtci-interceptor/tests/probe_cluster_padding.rs`.
- **interceptors (RTP circuit breaker, RFC 8083): a call's voice no longer goes silent for
  good after a capacity drop** (breaker-1). In a call between two peers of this engine a
  sudden drop of the path's capacity ceased the voice 145 ms later (seven voice packets
  dropped in a row at the bottleneck's full queue; the peer reports every 25 ms, so
  MEDIA_TIMEOUT = 5 reports), and with both directions capped, or a 1 s queue, the video
  (and voice) a few seconds later for congestion. Nothing restarted them. Read against the
  text:
  - **Restart (section 4.5).** "RTP flows halted by the circuit breaker SHOULD NOT be
    restarted automatically unless the sender has received information that the congestion
    has dissipated". The breaker now restarts a ceased flow, never before the triggering
    interval has passed again, on the receiver's reports on another flow sent over the same
    transport: packets of that flow arriving (media timeout); its loss over a whole hold at
    which the rate that tripped is within ten times TCP again (congestion); loss and round
    trip inside the application's bound (media usability); a report on an SSRC of this
    endpoint (RTCP timeout). A flow that trips again within ten holds of a restart is held
    twice as long each time (up to 64 times). When every flow of a transport has ceased
    there is nothing a report could speak of, and the restart is the application's:
    `OnCircuitBreaker`, then `CircuitBreakerHandle::restart` once `restart_after` has passed.
  - **The sending rate (section 4.3)** compared with ten times the TCP throughput was the
    average over all of CB_INTERVAL, which after a drop still holds what was sent before the
    congestion controller reacted. "The actual sending rate" is now also taken over the last
    round trip (RFC 3551: "The timescale on which TCP throughput is measured is the
    round-trip time"): the breaker trips on a flow that was above the bound over the interval
    the loss is averaged over and still is.
  - **The media timeout (section 4.2)** counted reports that could not have shown the packet
    they were held against (they arrived less than a round trip after it left), and went on
    counting for a flow that had stopped sending (a paused pacer); "When stopping sending an
    RTP stream, a sender MUST cancel the corresponding media timeout circuit breaker".
  - **Tr (section 3)** was smoothed twice in the default chain (by the congestion controller
    and again by the breaker) and trailed a filling queue; once now.
  - **Tdr (section 3)** was the spacing of the receiver's reports; it is the estimate of the
    receiver's calculated interval: what the chain's RTCP session calculates (RFC 3550
    6.3.1; `RtcpReportingInterval`), or the spacing of the reports where that is longer.
    Reports that come closer together than the calculated interval are each counted and no
    longer stretch the counts (section 5).
  What stays as the RFC has it: with a peer that reports every few tens of milliseconds
  (RTP/AVPF without a `T_rr_interval`, this engine's default beside video) five reports
  without a new packet of a flow that is being sent are a media timeout, in a quarter of a
  second or less. The flow now comes back when the flow beside it is seen arriving.
  A ceased encoding takes no share of the congestion controller's target
  (`RTCRtpSender::target_bitrates`) until it is restarted; dividing the target again for
  that sets the streams' shares only, so a flow that ceases or restarts while the pacer has
  the source paused (a target of zero) leaves `availableOutgoingBitrate` at the congestion
  controller's estimate
  (`interceptor_circuit_breaker_test::a_flow_ceasing_while_the_source_is_paused_leaves_the_estimate_alone`).
  Measured (the capacity instrument's cells, 300 kbit/s cap for 20 s; hosted runs
  45516841561 / 45516852677, 45516861432 / 45516870845; before = the same tree without this
  change): with a 300 ms bottleneck queue the caller's voice was silent to the end of the call
  in 63 of 534 runs, now no flow is ceased in any; with a 1000 ms queue it was ceased for good
  in 96 of 300, now the congestion breaker ceases it in 84 of 300 and the engine restarts it
  every time (silent 3.7 s in the median, 7.3 s at the 90th percentile, 10.9 s at worst: a
  known limit, `docs/circuit-breaker.md`); with both directions capped a flow was left ceased
  in 94 of 100 runs, now one ceases in 7 and is restarted.
  The capacity file's per-seed check that a sender following the target never freezes for
  more than 2 s (`a_sender_following_the_target_is_paused_and_loses_nothing_at_the_pacer`,
  retired with the capacity instrument in favour of its ensemble requirement) had been met
  in seed 6 only with the call's voice dead: there the breaker ceased the caller's audio
  0.166 s after the cap and it never came back, which left the video the whole floor (freeze
  0.98 s); with the voice alive that seed freezes 2.22 s (the link then carries 74 kbit/s of
  audio, 22 of new video and 91 of retransmissions in the pause). Over seeds 1 to 200 of that
  cell at the test's phase the voice was dead in 29; in the other 171 the freeze is the same
  to the digit with and without this change, and over 2 s in 14 of them (8.2 %) either way
  (hosted runs 45516852677, 45516841561). The bound is not changed and no seed is chosen: the
  requirement is the instrument's, over the ensemble, where it is a known limit.
  Audit rows RFC8083-3-1, 3-6, 4.2-4, 4.2-5, 4.2-6, 4.3-4, 4.5-1, 4.5-2, 5-3.

- **rtci, interceptor / RTP circuit breaker** (collapse-3): the application is told when the
  circuit breaker (RFC 8083, in the default interceptor set) ceases one of its flows. A ceased
  flow's packets are dropped until the application restarts it (section 4.5: "SHOULD NOT be
  restarted automatically"), and nothing said so: the state could only be polled
  (`CircuitBreakerHandle::ceased`). With a peer that sends a receiver report with every
  congestion feedback packet (this engine does, every 25 to 50 ms) a breaker trips within a
  fraction of a second of a sudden capacity drop (the media timeout after five reports without
  a new packet of the flow: 145 ms after a 2.5 Mbit/s path fell to 300 kbit/s in
  `tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs`'s scenario; the congestion breaker over ten round
  trips: 2 to 3.4 s), and the call lost its audio or its video for good, silently: the
  audio in 17 of 100 runs of that scenario, the video in the runs "that never show video
  again" of the capacity review (both directions capped; a 1000 ms queue). Now the breaker
  sends `CircuitBreakerNotice` application-ward when a flow ceases and when a restart takes
  effect, and the peer connection raises `RTCPeerConnectionEvent::OnCircuitBreaker` (sender,
  RID, SSRC, the breaker that tripped, how long until a restart is accepted). The pacer reads
  the notice too and no longer charges a ceased flow's packets to its budget: a voice the
  application kept writing took 76 of a 100 kbit/s target for packets that never left, and
  the estimate, bound by one and a half times what arrives, could not climb.
  `circuit_breaker.rs::a_ceased_flow_and_its_restart_are_announced_application_ward`,
  `pacing.rs::a_flow_the_circuit_breaker_ceased_is_not_charged_to_the_budget`.

- **interceptors (pacer): the target the pacer announces carries the congestion controller's
  minimum** (`conf/breaker-2-pacer-ceased-flow`). When a pause of the source begins or ends
  the pacer says the controller's target again application-ward
  (`Attribute::TargetBitrateChanged`), and it did so without the controller's minimum
  (`MinimumTarget`). The NACK responder takes the minimum from each target it reads and never
  tells the original media less; from the end of a pause until the controller's next target
  it read "no minimum" and lowered the target by its whole retransmission reserve, floor or
  not, and the peer connection reported that as `availableOutgoingBitrate` (46 850 bit/s with
  the estimator at its 100 000 bit/s floor: a 53 150 bit/s reserve announced before the
  target reached the floor; hosted run 45501349668, the reason `conf/collapse-4` was not
  green). The pacer now keeps the minimum that rode with the controller's last target and
  attaches it to its own announcements.
  `pacing.rs::the_target_the_pacer_announces_carries_the_controllers_minimum`.
  Performance: breaker-2

- **rtci (statistics): `availableOutgoingBitrate` survives `set_parameters` during a pacer
  pause** (`conf/breaker-2-pacer-ceased-flow`). `RTCRtpSender::set_parameters` divides the
  transport's target among the encodings again; while the pacer had the source paused that
  target is zero, and the division wrote it as the transport's estimate: the statistic was
  gone until the congestion controller's next target. The division now sets the streams'
  shares only.
  `interceptor_circuit_breaker_test::dividing_the_target_again_while_the_source_is_paused_leaves_the_estimate_alone`.

- **tests** (`conf/rtp-9-reporting-ssrc-intermittent`): the RFC 8108 section 6.1 test
  `a_receiver_that_starts_sending_sends_on_the_ssrc_it_reported_from` no longer fails about
  one run in fifty (28 of 1500 runs on master, alike under every crypto feature set; in CI it
  happened to show in the ring-only jobs). The engine was right. The test took the first
  packet of each SRTCP datagram, all that is readable on the wire, for the reporting SSRC's
  report. Once the stream sends, its RTX SSRC is a participant too (the congestion
  controller's padding goes out on it, RFC 4588 section 6.1), a compound packet carries the
  reports of both SSRCs (RFC 8108 section 5.3.2) and is led by the one whose timer expired:
  in the runs that failed the RTX SSRC led every compound packet sent while the stream had
  sender status, the stream's sender report second in each. The test now reads the compound
  packets whole, below the session, and states the requirement: from the stream's first
  packet on and while it sends, every report of that SSRC is a sender report (RFC 3550
  section 6.4); nothing says BYE; no SSRC reports but that one and the stream's RTX SSRC. It
  sends until the SSRC has reported twice instead of for a fixed number of packets. No engine
  change.
- **tests** (`conf/rtp-9-reporting-ssrc-intermittent`): RFC 8108 section 5.1 is checked in
  the RTCP between two peer connections
  (`every_ssrc_reports_on_the_others_with_the_setting_and_the_blocks_go_once_without`: with
  `rtcp_report_from_every_ssrc` each of a stream's SSRC and its RTX SSRC reports on the remote
  SSRC and on the other; without it the report blocks are carried once and none names a
  co-located SSRC). `report_blocks_from_every_ssrc_measured_against_once`, which asserted
  that the RFC form froze the video longer through a capacity cap on two seeds, is now the
  ignored measurement `measure_report_blocks_from_every_ssrc_against_once`: it prints the
  figures and asserts nothing, because that order is chance on so few runs (it failed with
  the order reversed under an unrelated change). Row RFC8108-5.1-1 cites the new test. No
  engine change.
- **ice: a working path whose round trip rose above half a second lost its consent after 30
  seconds** (`conf/ice-26-consent-late-responses`; RFC7675-5.1-7, -5.1-2, new row -5.1-16).
  **Engine behaviour change.** A consent request (RFC 7675) waited for its response four times
  the pair's last round-trip time, clamped to 500 ms .. 4 s; at the end of the wait its
  transaction was forgotten, so the response, when it came, was discarded as an unknown
  transaction: it renewed no consent and gave no round-trip time, and the wait never adapted.
  A path whose round trip jumped from 20 ms to 600 ms and more (a queue filling behind a
  capacity drop: hosted runs 45493039743 and 45493049553, four consent requests answered after
  785, 523, 608 and 918 ms) was `disconnected` 5 s after the first such request and `failed`
  30 s after the last answer that had come within 500 ms, with every request answered. A pair
  whose round trip was over 500 ms from its first check failed 30 s after it was selected
  when all its checks had been retransmitted (a retransmitted request gives no round-trip
  time, so the wait stayed at 500 ms); it survived only when a check happened to be answered
  without a retransmission, as a cancelled one is.
  Now a consent request's transaction is in progress for what RFC 8489 section 6.2.1 gives a
  transaction after its last request, `Rm` (16) times the RTO, where the RTO is the candidate
  pair's, computed as RFC 6298 does (smoothed round-trip time plus four times its variation,
  500 ms at least; `stun::timer::RtoEstimator`) from every request answered without a
  retransmission, and never longer than the consent expiry: 8 s at least, 30 s at most (RFC
  7675 section 5.1: "An endpoint SHOULD await a binding response for each request it sends for
  a time based on the estimated round-trip time (RTT) [...] with an allowance for variation in
  network delay", and "a response might be for a previous request (rather than for the most
  recently sent request)"). A response within that renews consent and teaches the RTO, so a
  round trip that keeps growing is followed; one after it is for a transaction that is no
  longer in progress (RFC 8489 section 6.3) and is discarded, as is, always, a response that
  matches no request the agent sent, fails its integrity check, comes twice or comes from
  another address. The same holds on the path an ICE restart keeps (which also takes over the
  consent requests still open on the selected pair; its own had no end but their number) and
  over ICE-TCP. Consent still expires 30 s after the last response that renewed it, and the
  agent is still `disconnected` when a consent request has gone 5 s without any response.
  What the RFC's wait does not cover: a round trip that jumps past 16 times the current RTO at
  once (20 ms to more than 8 s); `ConsentResponseWait::Fixed` does (see "Added").
  `iceCandidatePair.currentRoundTripTime` now also reflects the late answers.
  Found on the way and left open (audit row RFC7675-1-1, `partial`): consent is kept per remote
  candidate, not per candidate pair, so a response on another pair to the same remote
  candidate renews the selected pair's consent.
  **Known limit of 0.1.0** (for its release notes): a connection can fail 30 s after a path's
  round trip rises above 500 ms although the path works.
  Tests: `rtci-ice/src/agent/agent_consent_delay_test.rs` (17 tests),
  `agent_open_rows_test.rs::test_consent_is_kept_on_a_tcp_pair_whose_round_trip_is_long`,
  `tests/ice_consent_slow_path_rtc2rtc.rs` (two peers, the whole stack; three of its four
  tests fail on master d914b929, hosted run 45501729474).
  `agent_checklist_test.rs::test_consent_response_is_awaited_for_a_time_based_on_the_rtt`,
  which asserted the old rule, is removed.

- **sctp** (up-333): `ChunkForwardTsn::unmarshal` reads within the chunk's own length. It
  checked the buffer's length and read from the chunk's value, so a FORWARD TSN chunk of length
  4 followed by other bytes read a New Cumulative TSN it does not hold and panicked. Not
  reachable from a peer: `Packet::unmarshal` slices each chunk to its length first; a direct
  caller and the `chunk_chunk_forward_tsn_unmarshal` fuzz target could reach it. A value whose
  length is not 4 plus a multiple of 4 is an error, as for I-FORWARD-TSN. Found while checking
  the siblings of webrtc-rs/rtc#333 by @mitsuhiko (error-cause length and DCEP threshold
  panics), whose two sites the fork had fixed in 3866ed31. Test:
  `chunk_test::test_chunk_forward_tsn_is_read_within_its_own_length`.
- **turn** (up-316): a CreatePermission the application asked for that fails no longer drops a
  permission the server granted meanwhile. A permission is per IP address (RFC 8656 section 9):
  `create_permission` for two ports of one address before the first answer sends two requests,
  and when the first was granted and the second refused, the address lost its permission here
  (`send_to` failed with `ErrNoPermission` and the refresh left it out) though the server held
  it. The refusal is still reported (`CreatePermissionError`). Same defect as webrtc-rs/rtc#316
  by @hsdfat (whose other half, permissions keyed per IP, the fork already had). Engine
  behaviour change (TURN client). Test:
  `client_permission_test::test_a_refused_request_keeps_a_permission_granted_meanwhile`.
- **examples / stun** (up-954): the `trickle-ice`, `trickle-ice-srflx` and `rtci-stun` `stun_client`
  examples sent their STUN Binding requests with the all-zero transaction id
  (`Box::<TransactionId>::default()`); they use `TransactionId::new()`, which RFC 8489 section 5
  requires ("MUST be cryptographically random"), and `TransactionId`'s documentation says
  `Default` is never for a request. The engine itself always drew random ids (ICE checks,
  srflx gathering, the TURN client: `rand::rng()`, a CSPRNG). Same defect as
  webrtc-rs/webrtc#954 (webrtc-rs/rtc#283), in an application's gatherer there. No engine
  behaviour change.

- **interceptor** (fec-13): the RFC 8627 FlexFEC encoder no longer takes a retransmission on
  the media SSRC (a NACK answered without RTX, as after an answer that kept only FlexFEC, RFC
  8627 section 1.1.7) into its current block: its old sequence number broke the run of
  consecutive source packets, and the block went unprotected.

- **sctp** (sctp-17): two stream-reset faults. (1) A peer's Outgoing SSN Reset Request that
  arrives ahead of the last DATA it covers (RFC 6525 5.2.2 E2, answered "In progress") is
  performed when DATA or a FORWARD TSN brings the cumulative TSN to its Sender's Last Assigned
  TSN; it was then never answered with this side's own reset (RFC 8831 6.7), so the peer's
  channel stayed "closing" and the stream id stayed taken there, and the reset of a stream with
  no state here was not reported. It is now answered as a reset performed at once is. (2)
  Whether this side has reset its direction of a stream (so that the peer's reset is not
  answered with a second one) was the Readable bit of the stream's `RecvSendState`, which the
  peer's Incoming SSN Reset Request cleared: the stream stopped being readable although the
  peer had not reset its direction (RFC 6525 5.2.3), and its unread messages were dropped when
  the peer's reset came. It is now a flag of its own; the peer's direction stays readable until
  the peer resets it. Engine behaviour change. Tests:
  `rtci-sctp/src/association/reset_answer_test.rs`.

- A repair packet (RTX, FEC) that arrives before the stream it repairs, for a section whose
  SSRCs are not signalled (RFC 9143 section 9.2), is dropped without being counted in
  `discarded_rtp_packets` or reported by `OnUnassociatedRtpDiscarded`: its payload type names
  a repair format of the section, so it is not unassociated media (RFC 8830 section 3.1), and
  there is nothing to repair yet (RFC 4588 section 5.3 associates the RTX SSRC once the
  original stream has arrived). The likely source of the Firefox interop cell's
  `discardedRtp 15` with `discardedSsrcs` = its RTX SSRC (RTX by payload type, SSRCs
  unsignalled): RTX packets, probes most likely, before the first packet of the video stream. Engine behaviour change (a counter and an event; nothing was ever
  delivered from such a packet).

### Known limits

- **Stack copies of key material with either provider** (`conf/zeroize-1-dtls-srtp-key-erasure`;
  RFC 7714 section 13.1): building a key object leaves copies in dead stack frames, and the
  providers' own stack temporaries are not erased by them. The engine scrubs 32 KiB of stack
  after building keyed objects (DTLS); the tests catch stack residue where it reaches the heap
  (DTLS), and a copy deliberately moved onto the stack is not caught, so this is a measure,
  not a tested guarantee (RFC7714-13.1-3 `partial`, class E). CORRECTED (this entry first
  said the Linux process scan found none in dead worker stacks): building SRTP contexts DOES
  leave keys in the dead stack frames of the thread that built them. Train 34's test
  environment (rustc 1.99.1, run 45714962513) found, after the contexts were dropped, the
  SRTCP encryption key and its AES round keys, the SRTCP HMAC-SHA1 states and the master key
  (all ten profiles, ring; 120 key forms), in that thread's stack only, none in the heap; the
  same sources fail in 20 of 20 runs inside the test-environment image and in 0 of 40 directly
  on GitHub's Ubuntu runners (rustc 1.99.1 and 1.100.0): environment-dependent, the reason not
  identified (`conf/zeroize-2b-claim-matches-proof`). The
  copies stay until later calls on that thread overwrite them, or, after the thread ends,
  until its cached stack is given to another thread. An application can build contexts on a
  long-lived thread or call `crypto::scrub_stack()` from the frame that built them (it reaches
  the 32 KiB below that frame only). The process-memory tests now fail on any key outside those
  dead frames and print what they find inside them; the ignored
  `known_limit_with_{ring,aws_lc}_building_an_srtp_context_leaves_keys_in_dead_stack_frames`
  are the limit as tests (docs/test-exclusions.md). With the ring provider an RSA signing key keeps its
  private limbs in ring's own heap allocations, which ring frees without erasure (not
  measured). Until this branch, ring's AEAD, header-protection, HMAC, ECDHE and Ed25519/P-256
  signing key objects were also left in freed memory; they are now erased (Security).

- **the `Chrome` profile shows a stale picture after a capacity collapse** (red-2;
  docs/capacity-collapse.md, "The Chrome profile keeps its backlog"). Its pacer row is
  libwebrtc's (`pacer.queue-overflow` `Drain`): the backlog is never flushed, the source is
  paused and the queued repairs are delivered in order. One direction of a 2.5 Mbit/s call
  capped at 300 kbit/s, 1000 seeds, with the profile's RED video repaired (red-1, red-3,
  red-2): oldest picture 5.5 s, older than 2 s for more than half a second in every call
  (the default: 1.3 s, none); both directions capped 11.5 s against 2.6 s. Not a defect: the
  profile with that one row set to `Drop` is at 1.46 s, the default with `Drain` at 6.6 s
  (200 seeds). An application that wants the profile's other rows and a fresh picture sets
  `DefaultInterceptorOptions::pacer_queue_overflow` to `Drop`. The four-profile table of
  docs/capacity-instrument.md has the profile's column measured with the repairs.
- **a sudden capacity drop, with the backlog flushed** (`conf/flush-1r-backlog-flush-at-collapse`,
  docs/capacity-collapse.md; 200 seeds per cell; this supersedes the default-chain figures of
  the entry below): the default chain now meets the picture and freeze requirements in the
  standard cell and with a receiver without a bound in time (0 of 200; oldest picture 1.33 s),
  and the resume requirement after an outage with the bounded receiver (0 of 200); their tests
  are `on_demand_requirement_*`. Still missed:
  - both directions capped: 119 of 200 runs miss the picture requirement (oldest picture 2.6 s
    in the median, 10.9 s at worst; 200 and 12.9 s before). The estimate falls only by the
    rule for missing feedback; there is no backlog at the sender to flush.
  - a 1000 ms queue on the path: 109 of 200 (2.52 s in the median; 200 and 7.0 s before): the
    second already in the path's queue cannot be recalled; about 2.0 s is reachable.
  - an outage with a receiver that has no bound in time: 66 of 200 runs resume later than 2 s
    (200 before): no flush fires when nothing queued at the sender during the outage.
- **congestion control, default (paced) chain: a sudden capacity drop can freeze the video for
  more than 2 s** (`tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs`, the 300 kbit/s cap arriving at
  2.5 Mbit/s). Over 108 runs (six seeds, three wall clocks, six perturbations of incidental wire
  sizes and seeded draws) the longest freeze is 0.88 to 2.31 s (median 1.35 s) and 1 run is
  over the 2 s the test requires (4 of 108, 2.10 to 2.28 s, before train 24; one of them a seed
  `RTC_CAP_FULL` runs, so the full matrix failed then). Not a regression of train 23:
  `conf/jsep-75-session-version` draws the `o=` session id from the crypto provider, which the
  test seeds, and that one draw moved every seeded figure (with the draw removed every cell is
  train 22's again). The freeze is the repair of the drop's losses inside the pacer's pause;
  `conf/rtx-2r-smooth-limiter` (with `conf/rtx-1r-duplicate-repairs`) brings all 108 runs to
  0.75 to 1.28 s.
- **a sudden capacity drop (2.5 Mbit/s to 300 kbit/s), measured as its user sees it**
  (`tests/capacity_instrument.rs`, docs/capacity-instrument.md; master 63e1b8b8, 1000 seeds in
  the default chain's cells and 200 in the others; each is an ignored `known_limit_*` test that
  states the requirement, "in at most 5 % of calls", and a tripwire holds today's level; this
  supersedes the entry above, whose freeze counted any frame however old):
  - default chain, a receiver that gives a gap up after 300 ms and asks for a key frame: the
    screen shows a picture older than 2 s in every run (required: for no more than 0.5 s, in at
    most 5 % of calls); the oldest picture is 9.0 s in the median (10.2 s at the 90th
    percentile) and there is no new picture under a second old for 8.7 s. The source is paused
    about 8 s while the backlog written before the drop and its repairs drain inside the new
    rate.
  - default chain, a receiver that waits without a bound in time (the one
    `tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs` asserted on): more than 2 s without a frame of any age
    in 27.2 % of runs (that test's two to six seeds at one phase of the cap showed 8 %, and
    passed more often than not); the picture on the screen is 8.3 s old in the median all the
    same.
  - (no longer a limit, breaker-1: the audio never returned in 8.9 % of runs of the default
    chain, 33 % with a 1000 ms queue; now no flow is left ceased in any cell, and
    `ensemble_requirement_no_flow_is_left_ceased_and_audio_is_alive_at_the_end` guards it on
    every pull request.) With a 1000 ms queue the voice is still silent for some seconds in
    about a quarter of runs while the congestion breaker holds it (53 of 200 runs with more
    than 1 s without audio; 3.7 s in the median): `docs/circuit-breaker.md`.
  - both directions capped: every run of the default chain misses the picture requirement
    (20.4 s in the median), 8.5 % never show a new picture again, and the circuit breaker
    ceases a flow in 187 of 200; without the pacer 32 % miss it and 28.5 % never return.
  - both directions capped, why: each sender's congestion feedback crosses the other sender's
    overloaded uplink and is dropped there for about the first second (the queue drops RTCP
    like media), and what arrives is 0.33 s late, so the estimate is under 400 kbit/s 0.8 to
    1.9 s after the drop where one way it is 0.5 s. A missing-feedback timeout of three
    observed feedback intervals (RFC 8888 section 5 permits it) brings that to 0.8 s in the
    median and was measured and NOT taken: with one direction capped it cuts the healthy
    direction's target to 915 from 2373 kbit/s (audit row RFC8888-5-2).
  - a peer reports `disconnected` for 0.2 to 1.4 s in 13 to 17 % of calls through the drop
    (one ICE consent datagram lost at the full queue; none stays so, none fails): the
    documented meaning of the state (docs/conformance/audit/rfc7675.md).
  - without the pacer: the picture requirement is violated in 7.0 % of runs (interval 4.2 to
    11.4 %) and the freeze one in 5.5 %: at the bound, neither met nor missed can be claimed
    (their 300-run tests pass on one draw and fail on the next; run on demand).
  - a peer leaves Connected (ICE consent answers arrive later than the consent wait) in 16 %
    of runs of the default chain, and in 197 of 200 without the pacer with a 1000 ms queue, 3 of
    them to Failed.
  - an outage of 4 s ended by an ICE restart: in the default chain the next new picture comes
    later than 2 s after the new pair in 67 % of runs.
  - met: ParolNet's chain (no pacer, the TWCC-driven estimator) with the bounded receiver meets
    the picture, freeze and audio requirements (0 of 200; oldest picture 1.33 s), and the
    outage without the pacer meets the resume requirement (0 of 200).

### Testing

- **The browser loss-recovery cells no longer depend on who wins a NACK race**
  (`scripts/test-env/interop/scenarios.spec.mjs`, `common.mjs`, `examples/interop-peer`;
  `conf/test-2-firefox-loss-cells-count-repairs-without-the-race`; test harness only, no engine
  change). "loss recovery: NACK and RTX repair a browser's video under netem" asserted that the
  browser received RTX from Rust while netem dropped only the browser-to-Rust leg. The reflecting
  peer sends back the browser's packets under their own sequence numbers, so each such loss is a
  gap toward the browser too, and the browser's NACK for it crosses the same netem as the
  browser's own RTX of it: about 93% of those NACKs reached Rust before the packet did, so there
  was nothing to resend and the packet reached the browser as a late original. Firefox then
  counted no retransmission in about 1 run in 40, on the 0.2.0 release head and before nack-11
  alike (test-env run 45796440553; 40-run loops 45805447289 and 45805457083: 0 give-ups, 2337 of
  the 2338 NACKed packets Rust held answered). The cell now also drops what Rust sends
  (`impairFromRust`, netem on the Rust host), and asserts Rust's `retransmittedPacketsSent` as
  well as the browser's `retransmittedBytesReceived`. The reflecting peer now passes key-frame
  requests for what it sends back on to the browser's encoder (a PLI for the source SSRC, at
  most one per 200 ms), as a forwarder does: "loss recovery with the browser's SSRCs
  unsignalled" failed in 3 of 80 Firefox loop runs (and in 45796440553) with its decoder waiting, after one late packet,
  for the encoder's own next key frame (29 requests reached Rust, none went on).

- **The SRTP process-memory tests use keys of their own per test and classify every hit by its
  address** (`rtci-srtp/tests/key_erasure_process_memory.rs`, `conf/zeroize-2b-claim-matches-proof`).
  A test thread computes the keys it looks for on its own stack; two tests looking for the same
  keys could find each other's computations in a dead thread stack the C library had handed to
  a later worker (10 of 50 runs with two tests per provider, runs 45726164797, 45726174061,
  45726181744, 45726197738), the likely source of the one after-drop finding zeroize-1 left
  unexplained (45641590609). The worker is given its master key in zeroizing heap buffers; a
  hit in the worker's stack below its live frame is reported (`STACK RESIDUE`), any other
  (heap, other mappings, the worker's live frame and TLS) fails the test, and the live-key
  check now requires the key outside those dead frames. No engine code changed.

- **The released-sections gate compares with the newest release tag that is an ancestor of the
  commit**, not the newest tag in the repository (`scripts/check-changelog-released.py`). A
  maintenance release of an earlier line, tagged on its own branch after this line's last
  release (`v0.22.0+brainwires.5.1`, 2026-11-25), made the gate ask every tree of this line for
  a section its history never had. In a shallow checkout the script fetches the history first;
  `--tag` still names a tag outright. Tests: `scripts/test_check_changelog_released.py` (a
  throwaway repository with a release on main and a newer tag on a side branch), run in CI
  beside the gate.
- **RFC 4585 section 4.2: receivers do not rely on a reaction to feedback; RFC 7714 section 13.1:
  every key form searched for after the drop** (`conf/must-2-feedback-reliance-and-key-erasure`;
  tests and audit only, no engine behaviour change). `tests/feedback_not_negotiated_rtc2rtc.rs`
  and `sample_builder_gap_wait_test.rs::a_receiver_does_not_wait_for_feedback_the_sender_never_answers`:
  with no feedback negotiated and a sender that reacts to nothing, the receiving engine sends no
  feedback, audio is delivered in the `handle_read` that brought it, video after a loss is
  delivered within `DEFAULT_MAX_GAP_WAIT` and decoding resumes at the sender's next scheduled key
  frame (RFC4585-4.2-7 `tested`, out of class E). `rtci-srtp/tests/key_schedule_erasure.rs`
  (freed Rust heap, every platform), `rtci-srtp/tests/key_erasure_process_memory.rs` (the whole
  process, Linux) and `tests/dtls_srtp_keying_material_erasure.rs`: every key an SRTP context
  derives, its AES round keys, GHASH key and HMAC-SHA1 states, computed by the tests themselves,
  are found while alive and searched for after the drop (RFC7714-13.1-3 stays `partial`; class E
  after `conf/zeroize-1-dtls-srtp-key-erasure`: see Security and Known limits).
- **benchmarks compared on every pull request; a performance ledger**
  (`conf/perf-1-ledger-and-bench-gate`): the pull-request job "Benchmarks compared with the
  base" of `bench.yml` builds the pull request and its base on one runner and runs every
  criterion bench of both in alternating rounds (`scripts/bench-compare.sh`), and fails when a
  bench is slower in every round than the measured noise allows unless
  `benches/accepted-regressions.toml` accepts it with a ledger row (`scripts/bench-compare.py`).
  New benches: every DTLS 1.2 record cipher (AES-CCM, AES-CCM-8 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 added) and
  a whole in-memory DTLS 1.2 handshake (`rtci-dtls/benches/record_protection.rs`); the pacer, the
  NACK responder, GCC feedback handling and ULPFEC encoding (`rtci-interceptor/benches/interceptor.rs`).
  The once-per-merge run that feeds the published history runs on pushes to master only and now
  includes `rtci-dtls` and `rtci-interceptor`. `docs/performance.md` records every measured
  performance decision (accepted, queued or refused) with its figures, guard and runs; a CHANGELOG
  entry that moves a measured figure carries a line `Performance: <row id>`, and
  `scripts/check-performance-ledger.py` holds the tags, the allowlist and the rows' files and
  tests to the tree.
  Performance: perf-1
- **No test needs the public internet** (`conf/test-1-no-public-network`): on train 34
  `rtci-turn`'s `test_client_with_stun_send_binding_request` sent a STUN Binding request to a
  public Google server and blocked in `recv_from` with no timeout until CI cancelled the macOS
  job after 90 minutes. It and `test_client_with_stun_send_binding_request_to_parallel` now ask a
  STUN server on a loopback socket of the same process, which answers with the address it saw;
  the tests still check that the client sends a Binding request and reads the server-reflexive
  address from the response, now that it is the client's own address, and every read waits at
  most 5 s, then fails naming what did not arrive. In all, 17 default tests sent packets to a
  public STUN server: those two and fifteen `tests/*_interop.rs` files, whose upstream `webrtc`
  peer resolved `stun.l.google.com`, sent Binding requests to it and waited for them in its
  gathering. That peer has no STUN server now; both peers connect over host candidates on this
  machine. The two QueryOnly tests of `tests/mdns_query_and_gather_interop.rs` had connected on
  Windows only through that public server (the upstream server-reflexive socket, bound to the
  unspecified address, was the one path to the rtc peer's loopback candidate): on Windows and
  macOS their rtc peer now binds the mDNS egress address, as the QueryAndGather tests' already did
  on Windows. The engine-side ICE server of the rtc2rtc and interop tests (configured, never
  resolved: no test driver answers the engine's resolve command) is now `stun:stun.invalid:3478`
  (RFC 6761), so nothing could be looked up even by a driver that answered. Two loopback TCP
  reads in `tests/ice_tcp_active_passive.rs` are bounded. New gate `scripts/check-no-public-network-in-tests.py` (with its unit tests,
  `cargo.yml` Test inventory job) fails on a test source that names a public STUN/TURN server or
  connects, sends or resolves to an address off the machine; lines that only parse or configure
  such a name are rows of `scripts/check-no-public-network-in-tests.allow`, each with its reason
  and an exact count. Test and CI only; no engine change.

- **capacity instrument: the recovery as an absolute figure, the start-up, a cap that stays**
  (`conf/instrument-4-absolute-recovery-and-long-cap`): new figures `to1000` (seconds from the
  capacity's return until the target is at 1000 kbit/s; `recover` waits for 0.4 of the target
  before the drop, which is a different rate in a chain that met the drop lower, so it does not
  compare chains) and `startup` (seconds from the start of the call until the target is within
  5 % of the 2.5 Mbit/s maximum; 99 when not before the drop); new scenario `cap60` (the cap
  held 60 s instead of 20; measurement only). The baseline gains two tripwires per cell (the
  90th percentile of each new figure) when it is next recorded. Test only.

- **capacity instrument: how long a peer is disconnected, the direction that was not capped,
  a feedback outage** (`conf/instrument-3-disconnect-and-reverse-columns`): new figures
  `disc_time`, `disc_max`, `disc_open` (episodes outside Connected: total, longest, still open
  at the end), `stun_lost` (ICE consent datagrams that did not arrive), `low` / `mean10` (the
  caller's lowest and mean target after the drop) and `back_low` / `back_mean` (the callee's:
  the direction whose capacity did not change); new scenario `fbgap` (no capacity change, the
  callee's RTCP lost for 300 ms). The baseline gains three tripwires per cell (`disc_open` > 0,
  `disc_max` > 2 s, the 10th percentile of `back_mean`) when it is next recorded. Test only.
- **Congestion control feedback inside the RTCP bandwidth, measured on a call** (row
  RFC4585-3.5.2-5, a measured setting; the default, feedback sent as it is built, is
  unchanged). `feedback_inside_the_rtcp_bandwidth_halves_an_estimate_while_only_audio_is_sent`
  (`tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs`): with RFC 4585 section 3.5.2's timing for the
  feedback, an audio-only call's estimate halves to its floor on a clean link (5 % of a
  64 kbit/s session holds a feedback packet every one to four seconds; half a second without
  feedback is taken for over-use). The capacity instrument on the same seeds: one direction
  capped, nothing worse (oldest picture -0.33 s); both directions capped, recovery slower than
  20 s in 64 % of runs against 18.5 %. The capacity world's `Setup` takes
  `immediate_congestion_feedback`.
- **audit and capacity instrument** (rtcpbudget-4): RFC 8108 section 5.1's report blocks
  from every SSRC stay a setting (`rtcp.report-from-every-ssrc`: `StrictRfc` on, the default
  and `Chrome` once), now on the capacity instrument's evidence in place of a two-seed
  print: as the default it made the picture through a capacity collapse 0.53 s older
  (8.00 -> 8.53 s, 1000 seeds), the send target under the cap 24 kbit/s lower and three
  times as many calls slow to recover (81 -> 244 of 1000), because its compound packets are
  twice the size (RTCP of an endpoint 122 -> 149 kbit/s on an open 2.5 Mbit/s call). The
  instrument's chain token `every` runs it; the ParolNet chain of the capacity world takes
  `Setup::report_from_every_ssrc` too. Audit rows corrected: RFC8108-5.3-2 (an aggregated
  compound packet begins with SR or RR: tested, was "no aggregation"), RFC8108-5.3.1-1 (the
  conditional limit of two aggregated reports for non-updated peers: missing, was "met by
  not aggregating"), RFC8108-5.3.2-5 (untested, was "no step b"), RFC4585-4.3-1 (`b=RS` /
  `b=RR` of the remote description reach the session: tested, was "the SDP layer does not
  feed it").

- **capacity instrument: the behaviour profiles through a collapse** (rtcpbudget-4):
  `docs/capacity-instrument.md` has the table of the default, `Performance`, the default with
  `rtcp_share_follows_send_rate` and `Chrome` on the same 1000 seeds, paired: RTCP on the
  capped link 80 / 22 / 33 / 20 kbit/s, oldest picture 7.9 / 6.1 / 6.2 / 5.8 s, calls over
  20 s to recover 128 / 0 / 0 / 18 of 1000; `Performance` pays when both directions collapse
  (picture +1.6 s). The `Chrome` column was measured before the repair of retransmitted RED
  packets and is marked so.

- **capacity instrument** (rtcpbudget-5): chain tokens for the default chain with other
  settings, measurement only: `share` (the defaults with `rtcp_share_follows_send_rate`),

- **capacity-cap test: bounds from a perturbed ensemble** (`conf/capmatrix-1-perturbed-ensemble`):
  `measure_the_capacity_cap` takes `RTC_CAP_PERTURB` (the ICE SOFTWARE text absent, 27 or 40
  bytes; one or two seeded draws dropped first), `RTC_CAP_RULES=default` and runs side by side.
  Each bound says whether it is a requirement (the 2 s freeze: unchanged everywhere) or a
  tripwire, set at the ensemble's most measured and some 15 %: without a pacer at a 1 Mbit/s

- **the capacity instrument** (`conf/instrument-1-user-visible-ensemble`):
  `tests/capacity_instrument.rs` measures what the user of a call sees at a capacity drop and
  after an outage, per run: the age of the picture on the screen (oldest, time over 1 s and
  2 s, time-weighted percentiles), the longest time without a new picture under a second old,

  flows the circuit breaker ceased and whether a peer left Connected; over cells (default

- **`tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs`: the freeze and oldest-picture assertions are

### Test environment and documentation

- **video** (`conf/vp-9r-vp8-partitions`): the golden-stream tests of `rtci-video`
  (`*_ivf_survives_loss_and_reordering_intact`, `*_annexb_*`,
  `vp8_ivf_through_loss_decodes_bit_exactly_with_the_vp8_decoder`) no longer require 99 % of
  the frames decoded at 5 % loss, a figure calibrated to one packetization and one seeded loss
  pattern: RFC 7741's partition packets (every VP8 frame at least two packets) took 296 of
  300. They now state the requirement: every released frame decodes, and a frame is left out
  only when a repair held it up (its own, or that of a frame it predicts from, completed after
  the frame's packets were all due without loss) and a key frame after it was released: the
  frame buffer then released the key frame while it waited, or dropped it as too late
  (libwebrtc's late-frame drop). The VP8 frames skipped were 208 (repaired), 209 (predicts
  from 208), 239 and 269 (repaired), each just before a key frame. No pipeline change: no frame
  split at a partition boundary was mishandled. A mutation where a key frame drops every older
  frame, complete or not, fails them (VP8 260, VP9 154 released).

- **audit**: the library's advisory check (`.github/deny-library.toml`, no ignores) covers the
  published crates (`exclude-unpublished`); the whole-workspace check (`deny.toml`) now resolves
  every feature, so the unpublished crates' optional backends are still checked there. It
  ignores RUSTSEC-2024-0436 (`paste` 1.0.15 unmaintained, no vulnerability, no safe upgrade):
  an unmaintained build-time proc-macro reached only through `rav1d` / `rav1e` in the
  unpublished `rtci-video` crate's opt-in AV1 features; remove when those drop it. Recorded in
  `FORK.md` "Dependency audit".

- **docs**: `docs/video-pipeline.md`, the design of the video half of the media pipeline
  (`conf/vp-1-design`): what the engine already gives video, what a complete receiver and
  sender need beyond it, each element against libwebrtc (`a222406d`) and the RFCs / W3C
  specifications, the codecs available under the licence and pure-Rust constraints (with the
  H.264 / H.265 patent situation and Cisco's OpenH264 binary conditions,
  `specs/openh264-BINARY_LICENSE.txt` quoted), the crate layout, threading and A/V sync, the
  phases with their acceptance figures, and the decisions left to the owner.

- **stream-driver** (`conf/mdns-6-regression-test`): a return of 0.1.0's `PeerDriver`
  defect (the UDP sockets of `.local` candidates closed when the signalling state returns to
  stable) was caught on Linux only. `tests/mdns_virtual_time.rs` connects two publishing
  drivers on the mock runtime (whose multicast sockets now send from the address a transmit
  names, as the engine asks for mDNS) and runs on Linux, macOS and Windows in CI;
  `tests/mdns.rs` (real multicast) runs on Windows as well as Linux (on a Windows host with no
  interface that carries multicast to the group, as some hosted images, its two tests on the
  default interface print why and skip).


## [0.1.0] - 2026-11-24

The first release under the `rtci` names: the fork's `rtc` / `rtc-*` crates are `rtci` /
`rtci-*` (see "Crate rename" below and `docs/rename.md`), the repository is `Brainwires/rtci`,
and the version line restarts at 0.1.0 (crates.io ignores the `+brainwires.N` build metadata of
the `0.22.0+brainwires.N` line, whose tags stay). Since 0.22.0+brainwires.6: trains 11 to 19 of
the clause-by-clause conformance work (the audit's open MUST rows down to 16, every one
classified), behaviour profiles (`Rfc`, `StrictRfc`, `Chrome`, `Performance`) that govern 49
settings, one draft-conforming congestion estimator with the RFC 4588 section 7 retransmission
rule as the default, a pacer whose queue time is bounded and which pauses a source that follows
the target, SRTP re-keying that keeps the call when both sides' offers cross and loses no
packet, and data channels reopened on a just-closed stream that deliver every message.

- **Breaking changes**: the crate rename, and the API changes listed below by area (the GCC
  interceptor runs the default estimator behind the same `GccHandle`, retransmissions are held
  within the target by default, and more).
- **Known limits** (below): the cost of a capacity drop that meets the estimate at a higher rate
  (about 1.4 Mbit/s), the picture's age after a sudden drop with the pacer, the delay-side
  detector's blind interval after a sudden drop, and the margin a short SRTP key lifetime leaves
  for a re-keying.
- Fixed since brainwires.6's known issues: the pacer's unbounded queue, the circuit breaker's
  missing verdict for video flows, simulcast packets without RID or MID on SSRCs declared in a
  section with `a=rid`, video freezing for seconds after a capacity drop, STUN SOFTWARE that
  could not be turned off, and sender reports after a clock-rate switch on one SSRC.

### Crate rename

<!-- rtci-rename:start -->
- **Breaking: the crates are renamed from `rtc` / `rtc-*` to `rtci` / `rtci-*`, and the version line restarts at 0.1.0.** The root crate `rtc` is now `rtci` (`use rtci::...`), every `rtc-<x>` crate is `rtci-<x>` (library paths `rtc_<x>` -> `rtci_<x>`), the crate directories follow, and the repository becomes `Brainwires/rtci`. crates.io ignores the `+brainwires.N` build metadata of the old line, so it could not order those releases; the new line starts at 0.1.0 (tag `v0.1.0`) and the old tags stay. Cargo feature names are unchanged; W3C and IETF names (`RTCPeerConnection`, RTCP) are unchanged. Made by `scripts/rename-to-rtci.py`; `docs/rename.md` says what a dependent changes.
<!-- rtci-rename:end -->

### Breaking changes

- **interceptors (congestion control)**: one GCC estimator (`conf/gcc-4-release`). The
  TWCC-driven interceptor (`GccInterceptorBuilder`, `GccHandle`) had an estimator of its own
  that departed from draft-ietf-rmcat-gcc-02 in three places: the loss cut was applied to the
  delay-based estimate (section 6 has a separate loss-based estimate, raised 5% per clean
  feedback, the sending rate the minimum of the two), over-use multiplied the estimate by 0.85
  (section 5.5: 0.85 of the received rate), and nothing held the estimate to one and a half
  times the received rate (section 5.5). Under a 300 kbit/s cap its estimate was cut to the
  floor by a second of loss and climbed back at 8% a second, and where it stood when the cap
  went decided the recovery: caps held 14, 17, 20, 23, 26 s gave 945, 1192, 477 to 1316, 549,
  693 kbit/s twenty seconds later, the same under either retransmission rule (and on the
  release before). It now runs `Gcc`, the estimator of the default interceptors, behind the
  same `GccHandle` API (`GccHandle::stats` is new; `GccShared` has a `stats` field): 988 to
  1352 kbit/s twenty seconds after a cap of any of those lengths, 238 to 266 kbit/s of the
  300 used under the cap (145 to 200 before), longest freeze 0.83 to 1.24 s.
  **What an application polling the handle notices**: the estimate no longer runs ahead of
  what is sent: it is not increased past one and a half times the rate the receiver reports
  as arriving, and an estimate once reached is kept while less is sent (see the next
  entry). The estimator this interceptor had before climbed 8% a second whatever was sent:
  to 1.4 Mbit/s in twenty seconds of audio alone, and on to the maximum. Feedback that stops
  while packets are sent halves the estimate (`Gcc::with_feedback_timeout`, 500 ms); a REMB or
  a TMMBR from the peer bounds it.
- **interceptors (congestion control)**: an application that sends less than the estimate
  keeps the estimate (`conf/gcc-5-app-limited`). draft-ietf-rmcat-gcc-02 section 5.5
  introduces `A_hat(i) < 1.5 * R_hat(i)` so that the estimate "does not diverge from the rate
  at which the sender is actually sending", and lowers the estimate for one reason: "As soon
  as over-use has been detected". `Gcc` applied the inequality as a clamp after every update,
  so whenever less was sent than the estimate, with nothing lost and no over-use, the
  estimate came down to one and a half times what was sent: on audio alone to 106 kbit/s (the
  floor, with lighter audio: an application was told of a weak connection on a perfect path,
  and video climbed from the floor at 8% a second every time a camera came back on); on an
  open link by a step each time a key frame left the 500 ms window of the received rate
  (1 Mbit/s reached after 20.3 s instead of 15.6 s); after a path change from the start rate
  of 300 kbit/s down to 178 kbit/s within three seconds. Now an estimate at or above the
  bound is not increased and is not lowered (`ReceivedRateBound::LimitsIncrease`, the default;
  libwebrtc limits the increase alike, `modules/remote_bitrate_estimator/aimd_rate_control.cc`
  lines 235 to 249 and 266); over-use, loss above 10% and feedback that stops while packets
  are sent lower it as before. The inequality as a clamp is
  `ReceivedRateBound::Clamps` (`Gcc::with_received_rate_bound`,
  `GccInterceptorBuilder::with_received_rate_bound`,
  `DefaultInterceptorOptions::gcc_received_rate_bound`; `BehaviourProfile::StrictRfc` selects
  it). Measured in `tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs`, both chains: an open link reaches
  1 Mbit/s after 15.47 to 15.52 s without a pacer (15.82 s on v0.22.0+brainwires.6) and
  never steps down; a call whose cameras go on and off never has an estimate under the
  start rate, and video that comes back starts from the estimate it left (622 to 656 kbit/s
  when the camera went off, 637 to 674 when it came back five seconds later, where it had
  fallen to 106); after a path change the estimate does not go under the start rate.
- **interceptors (congestion control)**: over-use lowers the estimate on every update while
  it lasts, as draft-ietf-rmcat-gcc-02 section 5.5 has it (`A_hat = beta * R_hat` in the
  Decrease state); the default waited a round trip (10 to 200 ms) between cuts, which is
  libwebrtc's form (`AimdRateControl::TimeToReduceFurther`) and is now the `Chrome` profile's
  (`gcc.one-decrease-per-round-trip`: `Rfc` `false`, `Chrome` `true`;
  `Gcc::with_one_decrease_per_round_trip(true)`,
  `DefaultInterceptorOptions::gcc_one_decrease_per_round_trip`). Both forms hold every test
  of the workspace. Measured, the draft's form against one decrease per round trip: a
  300 kbit/s cap under a sender at 1 Mbit/s freezes the video 0.56 to 1.26 s (0.85 to 1.36 s)
  and leaves the oldest picture 1.68 to 2.48 s old (2.33 to 2.61 s); two flows that share a
  2 Mbit/s bottleneck have 0.49 / 0.49 of it (0.48 / 0.50) and keep a longer queue, 18.5 ms
  mean and 93 ms at the 95th percentile (2.8 ms and 10.8 ms); a flow that joins late has
  0.50 after 40 s (0.49), and 0.50 without probing (0.42); beside a TCP-like transfer the
  share is 0.22 with a 0.2 s buffer (0.19) and 0.25 with a 0.05 s buffer (0.37)
  (`rtci-interceptor/tests/rfc8836_multi_flow.rs`).
- **statistics**: `availableOutgoingBitrate` keeps the congestion controller's estimate
  through the whole of a pacer pause. While the source was paused, the NACK responder's own
  target announcements (sent when its retransmission reserve moved) carried the zero target
  without the estimate that the pacer's carry (`PacerPause`), and the statistic had no value
  until the pacer next spoke. They carry it now.
  (`a_sender_following_the_target_is_paused_and_loses_nothing_at_the_pacer` reads the statistic
  every 100 ms and counts a report without the member as zero.)
- **interceptors (congestion control)**: `BandwidthEstimator::on_unreported_packet_sent` (a
  provided method): the congestion control interceptor calls it, and no longer
  `on_packet_sent`, for a packet of a stream that negotiated no per-packet feedback (no
  transport-wide sequence numbers, no RFC 8888). `Gcc` counted such packets as "sent and
  nothing came back": audio without transport-wide sequence numbers, sent while the video
  that has them was off, halved the estimate every 500 ms down to the floor.
- **interceptors (congestion control)**: `Gcc` starts over from its starting estimate on a new
  path (another candidate pair selected) in the default interceptors too; it kept its
  estimate and restarted only the delay measurements. libwebrtc restarts likewise
  (`call/rtp_transport_controller_send.cc:356-357`, `restart_bwe`).
- **interceptors (pacer)**: the pacer tells the source to pause (a target of zero on
  `Attribute::TargetBitrateChanged`, `RTCRtpSender::target_bitrates` and the `targetBitrate`
  stat; `availableOutgoingBitrate` keeps the estimate) while the media it holds would take
  1 s or more to leave at the target, and what a source that follows the pause wrote is never
  discarded for its age; the 2 s bound and the whole-frame discard
  (`RTCPeerConnectionEvent::OnPacerDiscard`, with a key-frame request) apply to media written
  into a pause. Retransmissions leave ahead of new media, a stream's oldest packet first, and
  none is made for a packet whose retransmission still waits in the pacer. See "Pausing the
  source" on `PacerInterceptor` for what a target of zero means and how an encoder resumes.
- **interceptors (NACK)**: `RetransmissionRateLimit::WithinTarget` (RFC 4588 section 7) is the
  default of `NackResponderBuilder` and of `DefaultInterceptorOptions::
  nack_retransmission_rate_limit` in every behaviour profile (libwebrtc at a222406d sets no
  retransmission rate limiter on video and lowers the encoder target by the protection
  share: the RFC's form, see the profile table); `UpToTarget` and `Unlimited` are settings.
  Measured without a pacer (300 kbit/s cap, six seeds, three wall clocks): `WithinTarget`
  0.83 to 1.24 s longest freeze, 43 to 66 retransmissions of which 14 to 17 were dropped at
  the capped link; `UpToTarget` 0.84 to 1.29 s, 42 to 78 and 17 to 27.

- **peer connection, interceptors**: the `Performance` behaviour profile and the
  `performance-defaults` cargo feature (`conf/rtcp-1-rate`). The defaults are unchanged (the
  RFC values); `Performance` takes, for each governed behaviour, the cheaper form an RFC itself
  offers, never turns a capability off and never leaves what the RFCs permit (a libwebrtc value
  outside an RFC stays in `Chrome`). Measured with `tests/rtcp_rate_trace_rtc2rtc.rs` (two rtc
  peer connections, virtual time, 30 s):
  - `rtcp.t-rr-interval` 1 s (RFC 4585 3.4 / 3.5.3; RFC 5506 3.3 names `trr-int` as the remedy;
    kept local, not announced): at 1 Mbit/s one way the sender's regular reports fall from 13.2
    to 1.4 a second (27.3 to 3.8 SR/s) and RTCP from 4.20% to 1.45% of the media; both ways
    4.91% to 1.44%. Cost: report blocks reach the sender 1.2 times a second instead of 12.2
    (longest gap 1.36 s instead of 214 ms), which slows the RTP circuit breaker and RR-based
    RTT; NACK and congestion control feedback are untouched (120 ms to the NACK either way).
  - `rtcp.congestion-feedback-in-budget`, `rtcp.minimum-session-bandwidth` 16 kbit/s,
    `cc.feedback-share` 2.5%, `cc.feedback-max-interval` 500 ms: congestion control feedback and
    regular reports share RFC 3550's 5%. 24 kbit/s audio: 12.15% to 4.49% of the media (6.06%
    without `a=rtcp-rsize`); 100 kbit/s audio and video: 5.96% to 2.75%. Cost: at those rates
    feedback every 500 / 400 ms instead of 250 / 137 ms (Gcc settles 0.5 s either way at
    150 kbit/s, 6.0 s against 5.5 s at 500 kbit/s; a Gcc sender with probing fed by a
    `Performance` receiver reaches 2 Mbit/s in 0.62 s against 0.49 s), and a regular report
    only every 5 s at 24 kbit/s.
  - New settings: `RtcpSessionBuilder::with_congestion_feedback_in_budget`,
    `with_minimum_session_bandwidth`; `TwccReceiverBuilder` / `Rfc8888Builder`
    `with_feedback_share`, `with_max_adaptive_interval`; `DefaultInterceptorOptions` fields
    `rtcp_congestion_feedback_in_budget`, `rtcp_minimum_session_bandwidth`,
    `congestion_feedback_share`, `congestion_feedback_max_interval`. `BehaviourProfile` gains
    `Performance` (the enum is `#[non_exhaustive]`; `ALL` has four entries).
  - Cargo feature `performance-defaults`: `BehaviourProfile::default()` is `Performance`. With
    `chrome-defaults` also on, `Chrome` wins and the build prints a deprecation warning naming
    both. CI: a `performance_defaults` job like `chrome_defaults`.
  - Audit: RFC4585-3.5.4-2 is `partial` (was `tested`: the congestion control feedback sent at
    once is not added to `avg_rtcp_size`); RFC5506-4.2.1-1's note names the feedback that does
    travel reduced-size (transport-cc and RFC 8888 included).
  - Test environment: the RTCP cell logs the media rate it ran at (a few hundred kbit/s, not a
    video call's) and no longer claims the stacks report every second; the Pion peer counts each
    RTCP datagram once (its SRTCP session hands one datagram to every stream it names, which
    counted SRs several times).
  - The merge with master: `rtp.ssrc-per-clock-rate` follows master's default (one SSRC across
    clock rates, `Rfc` `false`, `StrictRfc` `true`); `circuit_breaker_packet_size` is listed as
    engine-only.

- **peer connection**: behaviour profile values verified against libwebrtc's source
  (`conf/profile-2-verified-values`). The 26 unverified Chrome values were read in libwebrtc's
  public source (`main` at `a222406d49ec`, 2026-11-23; Chromium's glue at `8dafa8bce175`,
  BoringSSL at `289645a45072`); each row now cites the file, the symbol and the revision. 40
  governed behaviours (was 35): 11 observed, 29 from the source, 0 unverified; 11 not
  expressible (was 10).
  - Wrong Chrome values corrected: `sctp.rto` is 500 ms / 400 ms / 3 s (was 500 / 220 ms / 60 s:
    dcsctp's `rto_min` is 400 ms, 220 ms is `min_rtt_variance`, and libwebrtc caps the timer
    backoff at 3 s); `gcc.threshold-time-base` is the new `ThresholdTimeBase::ArrivalCapped`
    (libwebrtc's `TrendlineEstimator::UpdateThreshold` steps over the arrival gaps, capped at
    100 ms, not the departure gaps).
  - New governed behaviours: `dtls.srtp-profile-order` (libwebrtc offers AES_CM_128_HMAC_SHA1_80
    before GCM; the engine GCM first), `sctp.max-retransmissions` (libwebrtc never gives up on
    retransmissions), and three new settings: `SettingEngineBuilder::with_ice_options_in_media_sections`
    (`a=ice-options` in each section, as Chromium), `with_default_ice_pacing_stated` (no
    `a=ice-pacing` for the default Ta, as Chromium), `with_dtls_flight_interval(DtlsFlightInterval)`
    (`Rfc9147`, the default, or libwebrtc's two round trips within 50 ms and 3 s). Also
    `without_sctp_max_retransmissions`. The `Chrome` profile's offers now place `a=ice-options` and
    leave out `a=ice-pacing` as Chromium's do; `tests/behaviour_profiles.rs` no longer accepts
    session-level `a=ice-options` or an extra `a=ice-pacing` under `Chrome`.
  - Breaking: `ThresholdTimeBase` (rtci-interceptor) has a third variant, `ArrivalCapped`; its
    `Departure` doc no longer calls it libwebrtc's.
  - Corrected notes: libwebrtc does not retransmit ICE connectivity checks at all (each is sent once,
    the 250 ms RTO is for server requests); DTLS 1.3 is not engine-only (libwebrtc's factory default is
    DTLS 1.3); flexfec-03 and RFC 8888 are behind field trials in Chromium; the doc of
    `with_unique_transport_credentials` now gives libwebrtc's rule for offers and answers (credentials
    per transport, shared within a BUNDLE group; its offers bundle every section whatever the
    policy).

- **peer connection**: behaviour profiles (`conf/profile-1-behaviour-profiles`).
  - `BehaviourProfile { Rfc, Chrome, StrictRfc }` (`rtci::peer_connection::configuration`), applied by
    `SettingEngineBuilder::with_behaviour_profile`, `MediaEngine::for_profile` and
    `DefaultInterceptorOptions::for_profile`; `register_default_interceptors` (and `_with_handles`,
    `_without_congestion_control`, `configure_congestion_control`) take the options of the media
    engine's profile, and the RTCP session a peer connection installs follows the setting engine's.
    `Rfc` is the defaults unchanged. `docs/behaviour-profiles.md` (rendered by
    `scripts/behaviour-profiles.py`, a Python gate with `--check`) lists 35 governed behaviours with
    their clause, each profile's value and the source of each Chrome value (9 observed in the recorded
    Chromium descriptions or the browser matrix, 26 unverified), the settings left alone with their
    class, and 10 Chrome behaviours the engine cannot express.
  - Cargo feature `chrome-defaults`: `BehaviourProfile::default()`, and with it every
    `SettingEngine::default()`, `SettingEngineBuilder::new()`, `MediaEngine::default()` and
    `DefaultInterceptorOptions::default()`, is `Chrome`. Cargo unifies features: one crate of a build
    that turns it on changes the defaults of every user of `rtci` in that build.
    `BehaviourProfile::compiled_default()` reports it. CI: one job checks the workspace and runs the
    profile's tests with it.
  - New settings: `SettingEngineBuilder::with_ice_software` (the SOFTWARE attribute of ICE checks,
    RFC 8489 16.1.2), `without_sctp_rto`; `DefaultInterceptorOptions` fields `rtcp_t_rr_interval`,
    `rtcp_immediate_congestion_feedback`, `rtcp_report_from_every_ssrc`, `twcc_rereport_received`,
    `gcc_threshold_time_base`, `gcc_one_decrease_per_round_trip`, `abs_send_time_on_audio`,
    `receiver_reference_time_on_audio` (the struct is `#[non_exhaustive]`; the last two put Chromium's
    audio abs-send-time and `a=rtcp-xr:rcvr-rtt=all` in the `Chrome` profile's offers).
    `SettingEngine::behaviour_profile`, `MediaEngine::behaviour_profile`.
  - Breaking: `SettingEngine`, `MediaEngine` and `DefaultInterceptorOptions` implement `Default` by
    hand (the build's default profile) instead of deriving it; `SctpMaxMessageSize` derives `Debug`,
    `PartialEq` and `Eq`.
  - Seven Chromium descriptions of the train 9 test environment are fixtures
    (`tests/fixtures/browser-sdp/chromium--*.sdp`). One of them corrects the doc of
    `with_unique_transport_credentials`: a Chromium answer without BUNDLE gives each transport
    credentials of its own, so the `Chrome` profile does too.
  - The browser matrix has five cells with the Rust peer under `Chrome`
    (`scripts/test-env/interop/profile.spec.mjs`; `examples/interop-peer` takes `?profile=`).

- **dtls, ice**: a new DTLS association runs on a new 3-tuple (RFC 8842 section 5.1: "a new
  3-tuple ... MUST be allocated by at least one of the endpoints"; section 6: "a completely new
  set of ICE candidates that were not recently used for any other DTLS association"). The ICE
  restart that comes with a new association (`renew_dtls_association` and the automatic
  re-keying that calls it, a data-only association replaced for SRTP, and the answer to an
  offer that asks for one) now drops the local candidates, and so does the new transport that
  replaces one an answer closed (every m= section rejected): it keeps none of the closed
  one's candidates, even without `with_discard_local_candidates_during_ice_restart`, and
  `add_local_candidate` refuses a UDP candidate on one of their transport addresses with the new
  `Error::ErrICECandidateAddressOfPreviousDtlsAssociation` until the next ICE restart that is not
  for a new association. The answer to such an offer lists only the candidates given for the
  restart, and engine-run TURN links delete their allocation and allocate again. An application
  gathers on new ports for the new generation. New
  `SettingEngineBuilder::with_dtls_new_association_on_previous_addresses(true)` keeps the
  candidates and the addresses, for an application with one fixed socket. Rows RFC8842-5.1-1,
  -2, -3 `tested` (`tests/dtls_association_new_three_tuple.rs`). The tests that set up a new
  association gather on new ports (`World::regather`, `Pair::regather`), with several
  transports too (`renewing_the_dtls_association_renews_every_transport`).

- **pacer**: media the congestion controller's target has no room for is dropped by default
  (`conf/pacer-2-combined`, `QueueOverflow::Drop`). `conf/pacer-1-queue-time` raised the pacing
  rate above the target to keep the queue under 2 s and released the oldest packet of a full
  queue over the budget, so a source writing above the target put all of it on the path: in the
  test environment (`testenv_impairment::gcc_follows_a_rate_limited_link`, netem 600 kbit/s with
  a 200-packet queue, a 2.4 Mbit/s source) the link's queue overflowed and GCC's target fell to
  its 100 kbit/s floor and stayed there, against 490 to 570 kbit/s before. Now a packet that has
  waited the queue time limit, or the oldest one of a full queue, is dropped
  (`PacerInterceptor::dropped`), and nothing leaves above the target; the receiver counts those
  packets as lost, which they are. libwebrtc's behaviour is
  `PacerBuilder::with_queue_overflow(QueueOverflow::Drain)` /
  `DefaultInterceptorOptions::pacer_queue_overflow` (exported as `PacerQueueOverflow`), for an
  encoder that follows the target. `tests/gcc_rate_limited_link_rtc2rtc.rs` is the test
  environment's case on the virtual clock (three seeds, 500 to 590 kbit/s held; 100 kbit/s with
  `Drain`). `PacerInterceptor::forced` now also counts the overdue packets `Drain` releases.

- **pacer**: with `PacerQueueOverflow::Drop` (the default) the pacer discards whole frames
  instead of single packets (`conf/gcc-2-frame-discard`). New media that waited the 2 s queue
  time bound, or the oldest of a full queue, goes with every queued frame of its stream (a frame:
  one SSRC, one RTP timestamp; nothing on the write path marks a key frame, so none is kept), and
  the rest of the newest discarded frame when the application writes it later. Retransmissions
  are still dropped one at a time; audio, audio retransmissions and padding never.
  `PacerInterceptor::discarded_frames` counts the frames, `dropped` still the packets. Each
  discard rides the read leg as `PacerDiscard` (exported; stream, sequence numbers, frames,
  octets, the target then): the NACK responder takes those packets out of its retransmission
  buffer, its waiting requests and its count of original packets, so a NACK for them is answered
  by nothing (RFC 4588 section 7), and the peer connection emits the new
  `RTCPeerConnectionEvent::OnPacerDiscard` ("the source is above the target"). A media stream
  also gets a Picture Loss Indication (sender SSRC 0) delivered to the application
  (`RTCMessage::RtcpPacket`, `OnKeyFrameRequest`), so an application that answers PLI writes a
  key frame at the new target. The pacer's order of service is documented: audio, audio
  retransmissions, video retransmissions, video and FEC, padding. Measured
  (`tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs`, default chain, six seeds, run 45300292535): one discard
  of 120 to 202 frames per seed and freezes of 4.3 to 10.3 s, worse than the 2.1 to 3.0 s with
  per-packet drops that the responder resent: the receiver's sample builder waits 256 sequence
  numbers past a gap nothing fills. Resending the discarded packets after all gives 1.8 to 2.8 s
  (run 45300304592). libwebrtc discards nothing in its pacer: past an expected queue time of 2 s
  it pauses the encoder and drains the queue (`control_handler.cc`, `pacing_controller.h`
  `kMaxExpectedQueueLength`).

- **interceptors**: the NACK generator asks for a lost packet while it is missing (a round trip
  between requests) instead of giving it up after ten requests or two seconds
  (`conf/gcc-1-cap-recovery`). The limits came with v0.22.0+brainwires.6 (`ee4217b2`) and froze
  calls: when a path drops to 300 kbit/s the sender loses some fifty video packets before its
  estimate falls, their retransmissions crowd the same full queue, and packets given up while
  the receiver's sample builder still waited for them left the picture frozen for 5.9 to 6.8 s
  until a key frame (ParolNet's `m1::the_estimate_follows_a_cap_that_comes_and_goes`, and
  `tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs` on six of six seeds). The limits stay available:
  `with_max_nacks_per_packet(NACK_SUGGESTED_MAX_NACKS_PER_PACKET)`,
  `with_max_packet_age(Some(NACK_SUGGESTED_MAX_PACKET_AGE))`; a signalled `rtx-time` still ends
  the requests. `NACK_DEFAULT_MAX_NACKS_PER_PACKET` and `NACK_DEFAULT_MAX_PACKET_AGE` are renamed
  `NACK_SUGGESTED_*` (they are not the defaults).
- **interceptors**: the NACK responder holds its retransmissions to the congestion controller's
  target (RFC 4588 section 7), read from `Attribute::TargetBitrateChanged` on the read leg:
  `NackResponderBuilder::with_rate_limit(RetransmissionRateLimit)`. The default is the RFC's
  form, both halves of section 7 (`conf/gcc-2-rfc-retransmission`): `WithinTarget`, the
  retransmissions take what the original packets leave of the target over the last second, and
  while they wait or were sent within it the target reported for the original media is lowered
  by a retransmission reserve (what the waiting requests need within a round trip, or the
  retransmission rate in use, at most half the target: `with_max_reserve_fraction`,
  `MAX_RETRANSMISSION_RESERVE`). The lowered target reaches the application as the
  `TargetBitrateChanged` the responder passes on (lowered in place, or on a carrier of its own
  when only the reserve moved) and through `GccHandle::target_bitrate_bps`; the estimate itself
  is `GccHandle::estimate_bps`. A request that does not fit now waits, oldest first, and leaves
  when the window has room (the responder's `poll_timeout` is that instant), while the receiver
  keeps asking for it (`PENDING_REQUEST_LIFETIME`). Near the controller's floor (the target less
  the reserve under the controller's minimum, which GCC now announces with `MinimumTarget`) the
  retransmissions take the window's room first. `UpToTarget` (a rate limiter on the
  retransmissions alone at the target, not lowering the original media) and `Unlimited` (the
  earlier behaviour) are settings. Without a congestion controller nothing is held back.
  Measured by `tests/capacity_cap_video_rtc2rtc.rs` (300 kbit/s cap, six seeds), longest
  freeze: the default 1.33 to 1.44 s with 65 to 70 retransmissions of which 11 to 14 dropped at
  the link; `UpToTarget` 1.31 to 1.43 s (61 to 65, 11 to 12 dropped); unlimited 1.04 to 1.58 s
  (257 to 367, three in four dropped); the RFC sharing without the lowered target 2.46 to 2.47 s,
  without the floor rule 2.46 to 2.47 s, with it only at the exact minimum 3.7 to 4.8 s. The test
  now also bounds the retransmissions (at most 100 through the cap). API: `GccShared` gained
  `estimate_bps` and `retransmission_reserve_bps` (its `target_bitrate_bps` is now the lowered
  target); new `RetransmissionReserve`, `MinimumTarget`, `NackResponderInterceptor::next_release`.
  A request the per-stream budget (one retransmission per original sent) refuses is still not
  kept.

- **media**: open media MUST rows (`conf/media-25-payload-rows`).
  - One SSRC across clock rates (the default since `conf/media-23-clock-rate-default`):
    sender reports extrapolate their RTP timestamp at the clock rate of the payload type sent
    last, not the rate the stream was bound with (`SenderStream` per-payload-type rates, RFC
    7160 3.2; Opus to PCMU had put 48 kHz worth of ticks on an 8 kHz stream), and the receiver
    places an RTP timestamp against a sender report or in-band NTP timestamp taken at another
    clock rate across the changes since (`MediaClock`, RFC 7160 4.2 continuity), so remote
    capture times and lip sync hold across a switch
    (`the_remote_capture_time_holds_across_clock_rate_changes_on_one_ssrc`). Reviewed and
    completed from the unverified `conf/media-24-one-ssrc-sync` commit 8cb42766.
  - RFC 7160 4.1-1 to 4.1-3, RFC 8834 4.3-6 and RFC 8108 6.1-2 are `setting`
    (`with_ssrc_per_clock_rate(true)`, the Chromium / WebKit cells of the browser matrix).
  - `RTCRtpSender::write_rtp_with_video_orientation`: the CVO element (RFC 7742 4, 3GPP TS
    26.114 7.4.5) on a video packet when the peer negotiated `urn:3gpp:video-orientation`.
  - ULPFEC send side: the carriage and payload types come from the negotiated description
